en: The Preface to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* concerns the wondrous truth that severs doubt and engenders faith, transcending all signs and surpassing all schools.
It is truly what is called the principle inherently complete, where the path of speech and thought is severed and the way of mind and intellect is blocked. It is the [revelation of] the Sage.
Since all things are fundamentally equal, there is no need for artificial supplementation or external seeking; what further use, then, is there for commentary?
Nevertheless, because capacities vary and convictions differ, one must begin from the low ground to ascend to heights, and start from the near to travel a long distance.
Without a ladder or a boat, by what means could one traverse the path? Thus, those who would climb the steep peaks of Mount Sumeru and explore the depths of the ocean of enlightenment—

One must certainly rely upon the sutras and commentaries to first attain the stages of hearing, contemplation, cultivation, and realization for severing delusions, thereby gradually reaching the inconceivable fruit of virtue.

Now, Master Yuan of Xitian Chan Temple in Wulin (the Master’s original name was Miaode; he had previously studied the teachings of the Xianshou school as a successor of Master Huai of the Capital, and later visited Master Tiantao of Jinshan)—

Master Yun was bestowed with the heart-seal (mind-seal) of Qingshan; because he avoided the taboo name of his uncle Xianglin, he was alternatively styled Yuanfeng. From childhood, he was exceptionally brilliant and wise; although he followed his father’s example and studied Confucianism at the age of eight, he was quick-witted and attained mastery over literature.
Free from any worldly attachments, he grew up under the compassionate guidance of Ming.

He established the four great vows as a solemn resolve and devoted himself with painstaking diligence to the study of a single scripture (his daily constant practice was the investigation of Master Zongle’s *Jingangduanyiwen* in one fascicle). He explored its profound depths and analyzed its perfect principles.

He then collated and cross-referenced the various commentaries on the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, scrutinizing them with the discerning eye of the Dharma. In all respects, none could compare to that of the Great Master Zongle.
To annotate means to make [the meaning] accurate and appropriate. Thus, oil lamps and sunlight succeeded one another, uninterrupted by cold or heat.

He divided the sections and explained the meanings, making this a masterful commentary on the entire work. In all cases, he took the essential purport of Master Le’s "Resolution of Doubts" as his primary authority for verification.
This is intended so that the scriptures may become clear as one’s own eyes and eyebrows, and their essential purport (*zhengzong*) remain unobscured;

it is nothing other than a desire to enable future practitioners to always view [the truth] as if looking at the palm of their hand, thereby gaining the means to investigate and clarify it, so that all may return together to the Dharma of the *Vajra Heart-Seal*.

For those noble and virtuous individuals with resolve who delight in cultivation herein, they shall gradually penetrate the meaning of the scriptures by means of these commentaries, and through the meaning of the scriptures, suddenly [attain realization].
By awakening to the Buddha-nature, one will swiftly sever hindrances and realize the truth, reaching the ultimate One Vehicle.
It is my hope that this will not render in vain the profound sincerity and vast benefit of the Original Master’s single-minded compassion. This serves as the preface.
Respectfully recorded on the Mid-Autumn Day of the year of Yiwei during the Qianlong era by Yu Zhaolong of Shicheng at Jingyi Xuan,
with humble devotion and prostrations.
Preface on the Lineage of the Nine Patriarchs:

Now, the Way is fundamentally nameless, and the Dharma is fundamentally unspeakable. This *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is the heart-seal of all Buddhas and the primary source of the treasury of the Dharma.
Although there are other sūtras such as the *Avataṃsaka*, with its principal teachings and attendant expositions, [this remains the foremost].
(With the *Avataṃsaka* as the primary [text] and other sutras as its companions,) they in fact do not transcend the Dharma of the Heart-Seal of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
For this reason, the Original Teacher Śākyamuni, before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, received the transmission of the Heart-Seal and entered directly into the state of non-arising.
Having reached the ultimate perfection of Bodhi and returned to the state of non-attainment, he further showed Venerable Subhūti that it was none other than our patriarch,
the Great Being Maitreya—
who is destined to succeed the Dharma King and has received the Buddha’s mind-seal— who could proclaim this flow of the ocean of Dharma.
It is said that he transmitted eighty verses of sublime gāthās to explain this sūtra.
Thus, Maitreya bestowed these gāthās upon Asaṅga, and Asaṅga in turn bestowed them upon Vasubandhu; through him, the profound meaning of these sublime gāthās was attained.

By dividing [the text] into twenty-seven sections, the doubtful passages are suddenly cleared away. Only now do the views regarding the cultivation, realization, and severance of delusions within the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) and the two sublime awakenings (*abhisambodhi*) become fully manifest.
The Way of the Vajra Mind-Seal (*cittamudrā*) has thus been transmitted from the Western Regions, and all these meanings have been thoroughly expounded.
Since then, among the translations by the various masters of the Six Dynasties, it is only the version by the Great Master Kumārajīva that...
The meaning of the text is indeed subtle and profound; yet, among the various masters of China who have provided commentaries, none have fully grasped its ultimate purport.

Only the Great Master Guifeng of the Tang dynasty attained this essential core, and thus he composed a *Zuanyao* (Compendium of Essentials) based on the verses and treatises of Maitreya, Asaṅga, Vasubandhu, and others to verify the intent of the sutra. However, the purport of this commentary is deep and far-reaching.

The text is concise; therefore, the Great Master Changshui—a descendant of Guifeng—followed the *Zhuanyao* (Essential Explanations) to analyze its structure and provide a detailed commentary, producing the *Kandingji* (Record of Collated Determinations). This work consists of four fascicles.
Later scholars, however, remarked that the commentary was too voluminous and its meaning too expansive to be mastered all at once; thus, various masters felt compelled to take action.
In general, one seeks ease of expression and proximity of meaning, yet both rely upon the text of the thirty-two divisions [of the *Śālistamba-sūtra*] to annotate this fundamental scripture.
Little do they realize that they are gradually obscuring the essential purport of the words of Maitreya and others.

Fortunately, during the Hongwu era of the early Ming dynasty, there was the Great Master Zongle, who was the preeminent leader among the Dharma generals within the realm, and who served Emperor Taizu.
By imperial decree, he was commissioned to examine the Great Canon and extensively investigate all the various schools. He compiled the essential tenets of the patriarchs, beginning with Maitreya;

these are characterized by concise language and profound meaning, where the phrasing is accessible yet the intent is far-reaching. Like the bright sun shining in the sky, their principles are complete and perfect—truly unsurpassed.
Nevertheless, although this Master’s commentaries on the texts that resolve doubts are clear and penetrating, they do nothing but omit the essential points.
Thus, while the phrasing and style are easy to read, the subtle meaning is profound and deep; those of shallow understanding find it difficult to explore its hidden recesses.

Therefore, disregarding my own stubborn ignorance, I have been moved by a keen desire to benefit others to divide the text into sections and explain its meanings, wishing to enable future students to view them as clearly as their own palms.
Should there be even a single phrase of error or misconception, I shall incur the guilt of being cast into the cauldrons of hell. Furthermore—
There is no cause for resentment.

Now, I shall provide annotations for the sacred names of the nine patriarchs of the *Vajracchedikā* to serve as a preface, so that all students may know their source and thereby initiate this endeavor.
This is the Preface.
The First Patriarch was uniquely entrusted with the Heart-Seal of Śākyamuni;
the Second Patriarch received the transmission of the Heart-Seal from his own teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha;
the Third Patriarch received the Buddha’s Heart-Seal and proclaimed the wondrous verses as Maitreya Buddha.
The Fourth Patriarch received the sublime gāthā and composed the *Treatise on the Eighteen Abodes* (Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra);
the Great Being Asaṅga was the Fifth Patriarch who transmitted the sublime gāthā and composed the *Treatise on the Analysis of Doubts and Explanations* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra);
the Great Being Vasubandhu was the Sixth Patriarch who translated the root sūtras without erring from the Buddha’s intent.
The Seventh Patriarch compiled the verses of the treatise to verify the essential meaning of the sutras;
the Great Master Guifeng, the Eighth Patriarch, divided the sections and explained the commentary, compiling a record of the essential meanings;
the Great Master Changshui, the Ninth Patriarch, annotated and explained the essential meanings of all the patriarchs without error; and the Great Master Zongle [completed the work].

Regarding the above (the names of the nine patriarchs), those who chant, recite, or lecture upon them must certainly offer incense and pay homage, praying in secret for their protective mindfulness so that they may accomplish their own practice and the fourfold eloquence of wisdom. As for those who serve as teachers:
This will not err from the Buddha’s intent. I pray that the noble and worthy ones will each carry this out accordingly. Thus, with prostrations, I write these words.
On a day in the second month of autumn in the year of Yiwei during the Qianlong era, the junior disciple of the Wu-ling [Hangzhou] school, the Śramaṇa Sa...
(name obscured), who transmits the thirty-seventh generation of the Linji lineage and concurrently practices the two schools of Chan and Vinaya, respectfully submits.
Recorded by Xingqi Yuanfeng at the West Heaven Hall.
*Commentary and Sub-commentary on the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Volume One.
Composed by the junior monk (śramaṇa) Xingqi of Qing West Heaven Chan Temple.
Revised and respectfully published by the Layman of Shicheng, Yu Zhaolong.
The Great Path of the Tathāgata, the Sage, is subtle and difficult to comprehend; Only those of stainless wisdom and clear vision can perceive it clearly.
Relying upon the sustaining power of the Buddha, I have composed this commentary to elucidate the profound intent of the Buddha.
May all ordinary beings universally attain the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Originally, the Way has no name; it cannot be entered without names and words. The Dharma has no teaching;
it cannot be transmitted without commentaries and exegeses. Therefore, I now proclaim within that which is beyond speech—namely, this very sūtra text—as its commentary and explanation.
This consists of two parts: first, the commentary on the title; second, the detailed explanation of the textual meaning. Now, regarding the initial explanation of the title, there are two sections:
a general explanation and a specific explanation. As for the general explanation: the full name in the Sanskrit language is *Vajraprajñāpāramitāsūtra*.
In this land [of China], it is called the *Sūtra of the Diamond Wisdom Reaching the Other Shore*. "Diamond" (Vajra) is—
"Metaphor" (*dṛṣṭānta*). "Prajñā" and so forth are the dharmas; this is a designation that manifests both the dharma and its metaphor.

Furthermore, the single character "sūtra" (*jing*) is the general title, while the seven characters "Vajra" and so forth are the specific titles; thus, it is named by means of both the general and the specific.
Regarding the second, the detailed explanation, there are seven points of interpretation: first, the three types of *prajñā*; second, arising from essence to function; third, subsuming...
This is used to return to the essence. (1) The fourth [point] uniquely reveals the Middle Way. (2) The fifth subsumes other names. (3) The sixth subsumes them into the one mind.

(4) The seventh shows the benefits gained from hearing the name. Regarding the first point, which identifies the three types of *prajñā*: Now, the diamond (*vajra*) inherently possesses the three meanings of solidity, sharpness, and clarity.

That is to say, "solidity" is a metaphor for the *dharmatā* (the true nature of phenomena); "sharpness" is like contemplative insight; and "clarity" is like the written word. This corresponds to the sequence of cultivation and realization.
The principle of severing hindrances: Why is this? Because by hearing the *prajñā* of words and letters, one attains instantaneous awakening and enters contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*).

One realizes that the phenomena of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are fundamentally quiescent and extinguished; thus, one severs the ten hindrances, realizes the ten suchnesses (*tathatā*), and reaches the other shore through the ultimate source—the *vajra*-wisdom of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
Furthermore, this is precisely the *dharmakāya* (the two characters "Vajra" signify this).

Prajñā (is the transformation of consciousness into wisdom), which is liberation (because it severs hindrances, realizes the truth, and reaches the other shore); for these are the secret treasury of the three virtues.
One is three; three is one. The existence and non-existence of the one and the three are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither unified nor distinct.
Second, regarding the arising of function from essence: the *vajra* (diamond/thunderbolt) is the essence, because its wondrous essence is eternal and immutable.
Wisdom is the characteristic within the nature of the *vajra*, because by transforming the eight consciousnesses, the four wisdoms are attained. Thus it is obtained.
Because it is the wondrous essential nature for the untainted enjoyment of oneself and others, the *pāramitā* is the wondrous function within the vajra-nature.

Since it flows forth moment by moment from its own nature as eighty-four thousand gateways of practice for the *pāramitās*, benefiting both self and others so as to reach the other shore, the treatise says:
"The Greatness of One Essence," which refers to the *tathatā* (suchness) of all phenomena.

First, it is great in terms of equality, because it neither increases nor decreases. Second, it is great in its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mahattva*), because it is fully endowed with immeasurable essential qualities (*guṇa*).
Third, it is great in its function (*karma-mahattva*), because it can produce all mundane and supramundane wholesome causes and fruits;
furthermore, it is said that this is the vehicle upon which all Buddhas have originally traveled, and all Bodhisattvas ride upon this Dharma to reach the stage of the Tathāgata.

Third, regarding the subsumption of function into essence: this refers to the various bodhisattvas who, in every thought-moment, seek to realize enlightenment by cultivating themselves and transforming others, severing hindrances, realizing the truth, and transforming consciousness into wisdom; until they attain entry into the Vajra-mind and reach the other shore.
It is utterly devoid of the characteristics of karmic maturation (*vipāka*). It resembles the solitary, full orb of the moon in the mind; for it is ultimately beyond the reach of verbal expression.

Regarding the fourth point, the "Sole Manifestation of the Middle Way": within the Dharma of the Vajra Mind-Seal (*cittamudrā*), the essence, nature, and function are inherently complete as a non-dual reality.
Because the wondrous essence and its application manifest according to conditions without differing in their characteristics, one is able to subsume the function back into the essence.
Now, when function is subsumed within essence, it is free from all marks. When essence is free from all marks, it is the Vajra Mind-Seal, utterly devoid of any distinct characteristics;
for this reason, it is called "Buddha. Regarding the fifth point, "subsuming other names":

the Heart-Dharma of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* is originally the Mother of the Buddhas of the three periods and the source of all treasuries. From this single name, all names flow forth—namely, the Truth.

Names such as *nirvāṇa*, *bodhi*, the true mark (*tathatā*), the eternally abiding reality (*dharmatā*), the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama, the King of Samādhis, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, the *Cittabhūmi-darśana*, and other scriptures—all emerge one by one from the wondrous meaning of these seven characters:
"Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā. Therefore, the names of all these scriptures do not transcend this source.

The titles of the chapters: the original titles of the chapters; the names of the various collections from which they flow. Tracing them back to their source until one reaches the ultimate origin, it is only through direct realization that one knows them.
Truly, they transcend the path of words and the sphere of mental activity, for the nature of letters is empty and ultimately nothing can be said.
Sixth, regarding the subsumption into one’s own mind: as for the Dharma of the Vajra Mind-Seal, first...
It is the fundamental substance of the body and mind of all sentient beings. Innately possessed by both self and others, it is without deficiency in either object or subject.
From the very beginning, it has been spiritually luminous, vast, expansive, and magnificent.
It is brilliantly manifest within the heart and mind, yet its form cannot be sought; it shines resplendently amidst sounds and colors, yet its principle cannot be divided. Great, it has no exterior.
Small and without interior, it cannot be seen through by the eye of wisdom that penetrates all phenomena, nor by the lamp of knowledge that transcends thought.
Thus, one cannot thoroughly perceive the such-like spiritual penetration of one’s own mind. Therefore, an ancient worthy said: "It is simply the original acquaintance from the very beginning."
To casually bring up [this matter] is already a mistake. Last night a gust of wild wind arose; how many peach blossoms did it blow down?
Thus, as soon as Linji had not yet entered the room, [Dayu] struck him out immediately. Had he not been broken through by Dayu’s pointing it out, Linji would not have attained thorough penetration.
Because he was broken through by that pointing, Linji cut off the mind, intellect, and consciousness in a single word, thereby entering the golden treasury.

This is the method for the Vajra-Mind Seal. Seventh, regarding the benefits of hearing its name: As for the Dharma of the Vajra-Mind, although it is fundamentally possessed by both sentient beings and Buddhas, it must rely upon cultivation and habituation (*vāsanā*).
If one does not cultivate it so that seeds are formed, how could one sever delusions, realize the truth, and transform consciousness into wisdom?
Therefore, by cultivating impure wholesome states, one forms impure seeds; by cultivating untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas, one forms untainted [seeds].
The seeds of outflows—namely, the vajra-seed entering the heart—how could they possibly be mistaken for melon or bean seeds? Thus, Qingliang said:

"Seeing and hearing form the seeds; the eight difficulties are transcended at the stage of the Ten Grounds. When understanding and practice reside within one's person, the fruit of vast kalpas is perfected in a single lifetime.
Therefore, when the Venerable One briefly heard the name "Non-name," he suddenly awakened to the ground of Great Perfect Enlightenment.
Birds hear sound and perceive form as non-dual and empty; they swiftly transform their retribution and realize the unborn.
This requires no great effort or extensive giving, yet one immediately transcends to the wondrous fruit. Through a single thought of pure faith, one attains the perfect realization of the Dharma.

Even the deeds of Śākyamuni Buddha, who served and made offerings to countless Buddhas over many lifetimes, cannot compare to this; how could other accumulated practices ever reach it? Therefore, I urge all who come here to strive.

I have studied this with great earnestness and given rise to a virtuous mind. Were it not for seeds planted through past affinities, how could I have encountered this Dharma by mere chance while seeking it even at the cost of breaking my body?
Alas! In these present times, people see it but cannot uphold it; they uphold it but do not understand it.
"To understand [the Dharma] but fail to practice it is like a person who spends all day counting treasures while possessing not even half a coin themselves;

what benefit is there in that? Prime Minister Pei Xiu said: "The devas are merely joyful, the asuras are just angry, the hungry ghosts suffer from hunger and thirst, and animals are deluded and ignorant.
Only in the human realm can one cultivate and hear the True Dharma. Therefore, for a human being not to practice it... [is a great loss].
There is nothing more that can be done about it. This concludes the first section, which provides a general explanation of the title.
△ Second, the detailed explanation of the meaning of the text: Indeed, a sutra cannot be understood without a commentary, and a commentary cannot be fully revealed without a sutra.
When both sutra and commentary are complete, the phrasing is harmonious and the meaning is coherent; they mutually illuminate one another. This is what is meant by "commenting upon the sutra."
I declined the honor of being selected for this task. My initial draft was too concise, yet I feared that the principles might not be fully elucidated;

therefore, I dared not omit the essential meanings, nor did I dare allow the prose to become prolix. Only when the expression is refined and balanced with substance (*wen* and *zhi*) do I venture to provide these annotations. Now, following ancient precedent, I shall divide the text into three sections:
first, the Introductory Section (*nidāna-bhāga*); second, the Main Body (*saddharma-bhāga*); and third, the Dissemination Section (*parīndanā-bhāga*). This is the first: the Introductory Section.

Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the *Saddharmapratyaya-nidāna* (Introduction of Testimony); second, the *Utpatti-nidāna* (Introduction of Origination). Now, for the first, the Introduction of Testimony:
"Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī... together with twelve hundred and fifty people."

Commentary: Master Zongle said: "Thus" (*evam*) is a term signifying faith and compliance; it refers to the essence of the Dharma heard throughout this sutra, which constitutes the meaning of the accomplishment of faith.
When Ānanda says, "Such a Dharma as this I have heard from the Buddha," he expresses the meaning of the accomplishment of hearing.
"At one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) refers to the time when the Buddha preached the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of his listeners—what is known as "Zengzi avoiding... [the rain].
The Master’s seat demonstrates filial piety; this is a time when teacher and disciple are in accord through the Way, striking and resonating in profound harmony.

It carries the meaning of immediate accomplishment. "Buddha" means awakening (*bodhi*); it signifies that the three types of awakening are fully perfected and all myriad virtues are completely realized, thereby being called the Ultimate Sage.
Thus, he is named Buddha, which carries the meaning of the Master of Dharma who has achieved perfection. [At] Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in the Kingdom of Śrāvastī...
Regarding "Guluyuan" (the Garden of the Lonely and Solitary): in Sanskrit it is Śrāvastī, which here means "Abundant Virtue" or "Renowned.
This is because the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) in that country are exceedingly exquisite, many people there attain liberation, and wise sages constantly emerge from it;
thus its name is widely known throughout the five regions of India. As for "Jishu" (Jeta’s Grove) and so forth: these are the trees donated by Prince Jeta to Anāthapiṇḍada. Anāthapiṇḍada...
The Elder purchased the Prince’s garden by paving the ground with gold bricks in order to invite the Buddha and provide offerings for both.
Regarding the phrase "the Jeta Grove," and so forth: the garden should logically come first, and the trees should follow.
The Elder was a minister of King Prasenajit, while Jeta was the king’s crown prince; because of this distinction between sovereign and subject, the trees were offered [as part of the garden].
This refers to taking precedence. It is the very place where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma; it signifies the meaning of accomplishment at that site.
As for the term "Mahābhikṣu," it is a Sanskrit word translated here as "mendicant" (qishi). Alternatively, it is called "one who terrifies Māra" or "one who destroys evil.

These are merely names derived from his qualities as a field of merit (*dakṣiṇīya*), a slayer of thieves (*vadhaka*), and one who has attained the cause of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Now, regarding why the bhikṣu is called "great" (*mahā*), there are three reasons for this distinction. First:

First, they exclude those who have not yet received the initial precepts; second, they exclude those who have not yet realized the fruits of the path; third, they exclude those lacking sublime eloquence. Therefore, those present now are free from these three types of exclusions;
having already realized the fruits and possessing immeasurable eloquence, they propagate the Buddha’s transformation—thus they are called Great Bhikṣus.
As for the "one thousand two hundred and fifty persons together," there were five hundred from Uruvilvā, three hundred from Gayā, and two hundred from Nadī.
The three Kāśyapas and their followers, totaling one thousand, along with Śāriputra and others, numbering two hundred and fifty, all came together to take refuge in the Buddha.
Having first encountered the Buddha and realized the fruit of enlightenment, they were moved by the Buddha’s kindness and righteousness; thus, they constantly followed his activities.

This refers precisely to the assembly that attained accomplishment through hearing the Dharma. From the beginning, faith was thus established, and the teacher and disciples were in perfect accord regarding their capacities; this describes the time of teaching and listening.

The accomplishment [of the teaching]. The Buddha, as the principal teacher, was at the place of preaching the Dharma in Śrāvastī, at the Jetavana Monastery. The accomplishment of the assembly and so forth are called the six kinds of accomplishment;
these constitute the *samyak-pratyaya-nidāna* (the introduction for establishing faith). They establish the basis for those who come to study, providing a point of reliance for every matter.
Placed at the beginning of all sūtras and universally present in them all, it is called the "Universal Introduction" (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*). Therefore, Ānanda asked the Buddha about all [matters].
Regarding what words should be placed at the beginning of the sutra, the Buddha said: "One should place 'Thus have I heard' and so forth.
It is not only my Dharma that is thus; the Dharmas of all Buddhas of the three periods of time are likewise. 2. The Prologue (Nidāna).
At that time, the World-Honored One, at the hour of eating, put on his robes... [having] gathered up his robe and bowl and washed his feet, he spread out a seat and sat down.
Regarding the "Introductory Section on the Occasion" (*nidāna-vastu*), it is also called the "Specific Introduction.

Now, while all sūtras possess an introductory occasion, the fact that this one takes alms-gathering as its occasion serves to symbolize that all sentient beings abide in dependence upon food. That is to say—
All Buddhas rely upon and abide by the Dharma of Prajñā. "At that time" refers to this very moment.

The World-Honored One (Bhagavat) transcends the three stages of the ordinary person (trīṇi-kauśalya), surpasses the sages of the ten stages (daśa-bhūmi), is venerated by those of the Three Vehicles, and is the common refuge for the nine realms;
therefore, he is called the World-Honored One. "Mealtime" refers to the early morning. "Donning robes" refers to the great [robe] among the three robes (tricīvara).
"Robe" refers to the twenty-five-fold *kṣetra-paṭa* (field-of-merit robe). "Holding the almsbowl": the Sanskrit term is *pātra*, which here means "vessel of appropriate measure.
There are distinctions between large and small capacities in *śronas*. What is now called "bowl" (*bol*) is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term;
it is the bowl offered by the Heavenly Kings. "Begging in succession" means that the Buddha’s mind is impartial, making no distinction between the poor and the wealthy.

Because he wishes to bestow benefits equally upon all through *dāna*, he begs for alms in sequential order. "The original location" refers to the very place of the vihāra within the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Regarding "washing the feet": this means washing the feet after the meal is finished. [Question: Since the Buddha is fundamentally free from defilement, why does he wash his feet?
[Answer: Birth is fundamentally non-deluded; it is because one pursues delusions that one becomes confused. Now, [the act of washing] symbolizes the destruction [of such delusion].
The false returns to the true; doubts are severed and faith is born. Thus, washing the feet to remove dust serves as its outward expression. Regarding "spreading the seat and sitting":
although the Buddha inherently possesses the four modes of dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*), the mention here of "spreading the seat" refers to Ānanda spreading the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat).
At the moment the Tathāgata sat cross-legged upon it, this constituted one of the four modes of deportment.
Consider this: the Tathāgata is the body of the pure *dharmadhātu*, fundamentally without arising or ceasing. Through the power of great compassion and his vows, he manifests birth;
thus, whether coming or going, it is like the moon appearing in a clear pond.
Whether emerging or submerging, it is like a solitary wild goose traversing the sky. Therefore, the *Vajragarbha* praises the Buddha in verse, saying: "The path of the Great Sage, the Tathāgata..."
It is wondrously difficult to know; it is beyond thought and free from all conceptualization. One cannot seek to perceive it, for it is unattainable.

Furthermore, it is said that "Nirvāṇa is the domain of the Buddhas' practice," and that "words cannot reach it," as expressed in various verses. This is what is meant by saying that before even lifting one's feet, one has already arrived at the great city;
before even stirring the mind, the Wheel of Dharma has already been turned. Why wait for Subhūti’s formal request for the Buddha to reveal it?
"Exquisite Sound" (Ghoṣadatta) refers to the discourse on Prajñāpāramitā. The first section, the Prologue of Certainty and Faith and the Introduction, is hereby concluded.
△ Second, the Main Body of the Teaching has four parts: First, the Request of the Appropriate Audience; Second, the Buddha’s Praise and Permission; Third, the Appropriate Audience... [text continues]

Listen attentively. Regarding the four Tathāgatas’ correct exposition, there are two parts: first, the request made by the appropriate recipient; second, the actual presentation of the questions. Within the first part, there are two sections:

first, the cultivation of reverence and praise of the Buddha; second, the formal presentation of what is asked. Within the first section, there is the cultivation of reverence and praise of the Buddha.
At that time, the Elder Subhūti was among the great assembly... [up to] ...well-entrusted to all bodhisattvas. Commentary:
The Elder Subhūti is the one who initiated this sutra. He is called "Elder" because his virtue is mature and he is advanced in years. In Sanskrit he is Subhūti;
in the language of China, he is translated as "Born of Emptiness" (Kōngshēng), and is also named "Well-Manifested" (Shànxiàn). He is so called because...

Rising from one’s seat and proceeding with reverence constitutes the respectful etiquette for requesting the Dharma. Regarding "rising from one’s seat": it means rising from one's original seat and approaching the Buddha’s seat.

Regarding "baring the right shoulder": the Venerable One drapes his *saṃghāṭī* robe over his left shoulder so that it hangs down across his chest toward the Buddha, signifying the non-dual unity of teacher and disciple.
Regarding "the right knee touching the ground": [this refers to] the right side...

To kneel with the kneecaps touching the ground before the Buddha is called *hukuei* (half-kneeling). In the Western Regions and other foreign lands, this is no different from the full prostration (*manli*) practiced here [in China].
As for joining the palms (*hezhang*), it means bringing the ten fingers and palms together without dualistic thought.

As for reverence (*gongjing*), it means harboring a heart of respect for the Buddha within, while externally manifesting the solemnity of the three karmas. "Rare" (*xiyou*) is a term used to praise the Buddha.

Thus ends the detailed exposition of the formal procedures for the three karmas. "Well-guarded mindfulness" refers to protecting and mindful of those bodhisattvas of the present whose faculties are mature, bestowing upon them the power of wisdom so that they may accomplish their own practice, and bestowing upon them the power of transformation so that they may gather in sentient beings.
"Well-entrusted" refers to having entrusted [the teaching] to those bodhisattvas of the future whose faculties are mature.
Those who have attained the Mahāyāna are caused not to abandon it; those who have not yet attained the Mahāyāna are caused to advance further.

This protective mindfulness and entrustment is a rare and marvelous matter. Although the Buddha’s virtue is so great that there is nothing superior to his saving of sentient beings, even as he focuses his attention on the Prajñāpāramitā for the sake of liberating beings, he must wait for a question to be asked.
Therefore, Subhūti, perceiving the signs and understanding the Master's intention, was the first to speak:
Having marveled at its rarity, he then asked his questions. △ Second, the actual presentation of the questions:
"World-Honored One, how should a good man or a good woman [practice], how should they dwell, and how should they subdue their minds?"
Master Zongle said: This is the beginning of the inquiry. Regarding "Anuttara" and so forth, in Chinese it is translated as "Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Enlightenment.
The intent of the question is that the Tathāgata, through his protective mindfulness and entrustment, causes present and future Bodhisattvas to attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
Although these Bodhisattvas have resolved their minds on the Way and vowed to deliver all sentient beings, they seek to achieve...
Regarding the Buddha-way: how does one’s mind abide securely in the Mahāyāna? How does one subdue the mind so that it reaches the fruit of Buddhahood without falling back?

As for the phrase "good sons and daughters" in the text, this refers to those who possess the five stages: first, the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*); second, the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*);
third, the stage of thorough penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*); fourth, the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*); and fifth, the stage of ultimate consummation (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*). Now...

This sutra correctly encompasses the two stages of the Bodhisattva—those of the equipment (*sambhāra*) and the application (*prayoga*)—gradually leading them to penetration until they reach the ultimate stage.
II. The Tathāgata’s Commendation.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent" (up to) "you should abide thus and thus subdue your mind.
Commentary: Since Subhūti had truly requested [instruction] in accordance with the Buddha’s sublime mind, the Buddha confirmed it by saying "excellent.
He then declared, "I shall explain it for you," and further cautioned him, saying, "You should abide thus and thus subdue your mind"; this refers to the Buddha’s own [teaching].
The words of mind-to-mind transmission and intention-to-intention entrustment are to be discerned within the state of expectant listening. △ Third, the responsive audience’s expectant listening:
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One; we wish and desire to hear. Commentary:
Because the Buddha displayed these two characters, “Thus” (evam), their meaning contains the attainment of the non-abiding mind, which is termed the "Buddha-abode. To realize this...
Obstruction is itself reality; this is called "subduing the mind. Thus, Subhūti immediately grasped the Buddha’s intention and responded with assent, saying, "Yes, World-Honored One.

Just as when Confucius showed his disciples the "single thread" that unifies all, and Zengzi replied, "Yes," suddenly penetrating the Dharma-seal of Zhongni’s mind, so too did the Venerable One, beneath the Buddha’s words, attain total clarity of mind.
The source is as stated in the following passage: "Through momentary pure faith, one attains the perfect realization of the Dharma.
Therefore, the Venerable One made this request, desiring that the Buddha explain it in detail for the broad benefit of the multitude; thus he said, "I wish and delight to hear it.

"Wishing and delighting" pertains to the wisdom of faith (*śraddhā-prajñā*), while "hearing" refers to the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*). This so-called seeking of the ultimate truth without relying on words and letters is what constitutes true hearing.
The Ear of Wisdom. △ Fourth, the Tathāgata’s Correct Exposition, which has two parts: first, the direct answer to the question; second, following up to sever doubts.
First, the direct answer to the question, which has two parts: first, the answer regarding the subduing of the mind, which further has two parts: first, the heading.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this manner. [Commentary: "Bodhisattva" is a Sanskrit term;
in this land [of China], it is called "Awakened Sentient Being" (Jue Youqing). This means that one has deeply awakened to the Buddha-nature, yet their afflictions (*kleśa*) are not yet purified;
thus, they are named "Awakened Sentient Beings. "Mahāsattva" is, in this land, called "Great Being" (Dasheng), which refers to the mind of the Great Way (*mahāyāna-citta*).

Sentient beings—these are the Great Bodhisattvas among bodhisattvas. That is to say, they believe in the Mahāyāna, understand the Great Dharma, cultivate the Great Practice, and realize the Great Fruit;
for these reasons, they are designated by the title "Great Beings" (Mahāsattva). △ Second, the explanation of the divisions has four parts:
first, the vast mind; second, the foremost mind; third, the constant mind; fourth, the non-perverted mind. Now, first, the vast mind.
"All classes of sentient beings" (up to) "neither with perception nor without perception.

Commentary: Master Zongle says: Humans and animals possess all four modes of birth (*yoni*). Those in the heavens, the hells, and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)—these three—are born by transformation (*aupapāduka*).

Ghosts may be born from a womb or by transformation; these all belong to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). If they possess form, they belong to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). [The fourth is the Formless Realm.]
The dhyāna heavens. If they are formless, they are the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the four heavens of emptiness (*ākāśānantyāyatana*, etc.).

What is now called "with perception" refers to the heaven of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) among the four heavens of emptiness. "Without perception" refers to the heaven of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) among the four heavens of emptiness.
As for "neither with perception nor without perception," this is the heaven that constitutes the ultimate summit within the four heavens of emptiness. This heaven...
By the power of the four dhyānas and the eight attainments of the formless realm, it is like water turning to ice, freezing all fish and grass so that they may not move;
the temporary cessation of the various consciousnesses is likewise. That is to say, the previously evolving consciousnesses are entirely exhausted, leaving only the nature of the ālayavijñāna.
Whether one considers them as existing or as having perished: if one considers them, although coarse perceptions have been extinguished, subtle perceptions have not yet been eliminated. If...

They pass away. Because their subtle conceptualizations have not yet been eliminated, their consciousness suddenly ceases to manifest; thus, while dwelling in this heaven, they falsely reckon it to be *nirvāṇa* and consider it their own attainment.
Thinking, "Among all people in the world, there is none like me," they give rise to great *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am").

Consequently, they remain within the ground of ignorance and self-love, and having not yet escaped birth and death, when their retribution is exhausted, they fall back again into the realms of transmigration. Bodhi...
Upon seeing this, he gave rise to a mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), desiring to deliver all immeasurable sentient beings within the three realms.
This is what constitutes the "vast mind. △ Second, the foremost mind.
"I shall cause them all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to final liberation.

[Commentary: *Nirvāṇa* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "Perfect Stillness" (*yuánjì*) or "Extinction and Liberation" (*mièdù*). There are four types of *nirvāṇa*: first, *svabhāva-nirvāṇa* (intrinsic *nirvāṇa*);
second, *apratisthita-nirvāṇa* (non-abiding *nirvāṇa*); third, *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (*nirvāṇa* with remainder); and fourth, *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (*nirvāṇa* without remainder). First...

This is common to both ordinary beings and sages. Second are the response-transformations of the Buddhas. Third are those with minor fruits, who have only severed the views and afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms but have not yet escaped ignorance.
Fourth are those who have already escaped them completely; hence they are called "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*). However, as for the great beings who wish to deliver sentient beings:
He then employs a specific dharma—namely, the dharma of nirvāṇa—to bring them to extinction.
However, although they attain nirvāṇa, if it is not the Great Nirvāṇa (mahāparinirvāṇa), what benefit would there be in delivering sentient beings?
It is precisely because he now wishes to cause all sentient beings to enter the Great Nirvāṇa without remainder that this constitutes the first mind of a bodhisattva. △ Third, the Mind of Constancy.
"In this way, although I have brought immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, in reality there are no sentient beings who have attained parinirvāṇa.
Commentary: Although the Great Being has generated a most excellent resolve, desiring to lead all sentient beings into nirvana, he fears that the views of self and other have not yet been emptied.
Therefore, he cultivates the two gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, which means to deliver [beings] in every thought-moment.
At the time of birth, in reality, there are no sentient beings who attain extinction. To deliver sentient beings in every thought-moment, one realizes that birth is itself an illusion;

that which is not an illusion does not arise. This is the contemplation of the provisional (parikalpita). To realize in every thought-moment that there is truly no birth to be delivered is the contemplation of emptiness (śūnyatā).

This is what is meant by "neither abiding in emptiness nor in existence," where both truths are simultaneously forgotten. One realizes that sentient beings and Buddhas are identical in suchness (*tathatā*), and reflects upon self and other within non-duality.
Second, all views are naturally eliminated because all phenomena are fundamentally and eternally quiescent;
this is what is called the "ever-abiding mind. Fourth, the non-perverted mind.
Why is this? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva [up to] possesses the mark of a self, he is not a bodhisattva.
Commentary: If one possesses the four marks, these are called the four inversions. Master Zongle said:

"If one does not cause all sentient beings to attain parinirvāṇa, yet perceives that sentient beings have truly attained parinirvāṇa, then one has not yet fully realized the fundamental source. Thus...
One who possesses the four marks of self, person, sentient being, and life-span is not called a bodhisattva.

"Self" refers to the false conceptualization of a self and what belongs to a self within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). "Person" refers to the false conceptualization that one is born as a human being, distinct from other realms of existence.

"Sentient being" refers to the false conceptualization that one is born through the combination of the five aggregates. "Life-span" refers to the false conceptualization that one experiences the fruits of a single lifetime.
"Retribution" refers to the fruits of karma over a single lifetime, whether long or short; this is "life span. All of these are inverted false conceptions and are also termed the "four views.

When a Mahāsattva employs the wondrous wisdom of non-arising *prajñā* to realize that the aggregates, bases, and elements are fundamentally quiescent and devoid of all marks, it is called "subduing the mind"; thus, there is no longer an inverted mind. Otherwise, [it would not be so].
He is not a bodhisattva. △ Next, the answer concerning abiding in wondrous conduct has three parts: first, the direct answer regarding non-abiding; second, the manifestation of benefits;
third, the summary conclusion. Now, the first part: the direct answer regarding non-abiding.
Furthermore, Subhūti... (up to)... a bodhisattva should practice giving in this way, not dwelling upon signs.

[Commentary: "One should have no dwelling place" means that when practicing the various perfections such as giving, the mind does not dwell upon the signs or conceptualizations of the objects of the six sense-fields.
This is because, in every thought-moment, one constantly practices the wondrous principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and the conduct of quiescent extinction. Now, as for giving...
Regarding the meaning of practice: it fundamentally comprises the practices of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). Thus, the verse of Maitreya says: "The meaning of *dāna* encompasses the six:

material gifts, the gift of fearlessness, and the gift of Dharma; herein, the first, second, and third are called the abodes of cultivation. The first, the gift of material goods (*āmiṣadāna*), subsumes the first perfection.
The second, the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*), subsumes the middle two perfections—namely, ethical discipline (*śīla*) and patience (*kṣānti*).

They afflict sentient beings; yet through patience, they do not retaliate against those who harbor enmity. Third is the gift of Dharma, which subsumes the latter three perfections: namely, teaching the Dharma with tireless diligence;
teaching the Dharma with meditative concentration that does not miss the opportune moment; and teaching the Dharma with wisdom that is free from inversion.

Furthermore, these three types of giving do not transcend the objective conditions of the six sense objects. They provide for the necessities of life, grant fearlessness, and bring about a thorough realization of both the internal and external.
In the interim, the three wheels are empty of intrinsic nature; therefore, one does not abide in the increase of the six sense objects.

Because one realizes that all phenomena—the mind, its objects, the grasper, and the grasped—are entirely without self, their intrinsic nature is fundamentally unborn, emptiness, and perfect quiescence.
Regarding the gift of Dharma: when the teacher expounds the Dharma, they do not grasp at signs and remain unmoving in suchness. By means of this bodhi-...

Because the Bodhisattva does not dwell upon the marks or conceptions of the six sense objects, and because his mind is free from grasping as he practices the sublime principle of the emptiness and quiescence of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*), the verse says:

"This is called dwelling in practice. Because one cultivates the two gates of śamatha and vipaśyanā through this sublime principle, severing the ten obstacles and realizing the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*), it is called "dwelling in practice. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva does not practice giving for the sake of his own self.
[He] practices. He does not practice giving for the sake of repaying kindness, nor does he practice giving for the sake of karmic retribution.

Because the Buddha fears that the Bodhisattva might give rise to greed, anger, delusion, or craving within the phenomena of the six sense objects—thereby creating obstacles to the death-and-rebirth of fragmentation (*prādeśika-maraṇa*) and the death-and-rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāma-maraṇa*), as well as various other hindrances—he again addressed Śūnyatājanman, saying:
A bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner, not dwelling on signs. △ Second, revealing the benefits and severing doubts:
Why is this? If a bodhisattva does not dwell on signs... (as far as) it is likewise inconceivable.

Commentary: Master Zongle said: "I fear this section may give rise to doubt, thinking: 'If one practices giving and other deeds without abiding in signs, then one is practicing with detachment from signs;
if so, there would be no karmic reward. Therefore, the Buddha refutes this doubt by saying that the merit of giving detached from signs is even greater.
This is because such practices as giving without abiding in signs accord with the emptiness of nature (dharmatā-śūnyatā). Thus, it is [the merit of] the emptiness of nature..."
It is quiescent. Because the merit of giving is free from marks (*animitta*) and likewise boundless, even the empty space of the ten directions is difficult to use as a metaphor for it.
The *Śāstra* states: "The metaphors for empty space have three meanings: first, pervading all; second, being vast, expansive, and lofty;
third, being ultimately inexhaustible. These three metaphors for the wheel [of dharma] encompass the essence of the Dharma and also fully contain these three meanings.
[End of section] △ Third, the conclusion on the benefit of abiding accordingly.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should only abide as instructed.
*Commentary*: "Abiding as instructed" means abiding in accordance with the various practices, such as non-abiding, the signless, and the wishless, which I have demonstrated above.

This is to profoundly accord with the nature of the wondrous principle of signlessness—namely, the severing of hindrances and the realization of truth. This constitutes the true dwelling of the Bodhisattva;
thus concludes the preceding section on "Subduing and Abiding."
△ Commentary: Second, summarizing the traces and severing doubts. The text is divided into twenty-seven sections of doubtful points.

Fearing that when Bodhisattvas cultivate various sublime practices, they might fall into the grasping of signs regarding the diverse phenomena of the views of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the text therefore severs doubts at every stage to sweep away all such views.
As Maitreya’s verse says: "In subduing those objects... [far removed].

This involves departing from the mind that grasps at signs and severing various doubts, while also preventing the arising of such a mind. Herein, first is the severing of the doubt regarding the grasping for signs when practicing giving with the aspiration for Buddhahood.
This doubt arises from the preceding passage on "giving without dwelling upon signs. The text is divided into three parts;
first, the inquiry poses a counter-interrogation to investigate the doubt.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of his physical marks? The Commentary states:
To sever doubts, it is said that the Buddha feared the Venerable One might give rise to suspicion, thinking: "Previously, he practiced the giving of non-abiding marks;
this was a causal practice of formlessness. How is it that today, upon seeing the Buddha achieve enlightenment, he again perceives a fruit characterized by form?"
Therefore, he took up these words and questioned the Venerable One, saying: "Can [the Buddha] be seen by means of his physical marks (rūpalakṣaṇa), and so forth?
△ Second, resolving doubts and realizing the vision.
"No, World-Honored One. It is not by means of physical marks [that one sees the Tathāgata]. As the Tathāgata has said, 'physical marks' are themselves 'not physical marks.
Commentary: Because the Venerable One, upon briefly hearing and probing the words, immediately grasped the Buddha’s intent, he did not perceive the Tathāgata while abiding in physical marks.
By thoroughly understanding that marks are themselves non-marks, he beheld the essence of the Buddha-Dharma. (3)
To further explain and clarify the manifestation of truth, the Buddha told Subhūti: "Whatever has marks... if one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, fearing that although the Venerable One had awakened to the principle of signlessness (*animitta*), he had not yet attained the thorough purification of the seeds of doubt, [the Buddha] spoke again.
The text for dispelling doubts states: "Whatever you perceive is entirely within the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

If, upon encountering reality, you realize that appearances are non-appearances, you will see the mark of ultimate reality. This is what is meant by 'the dependent nature being without self-nature is itself the essence of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Therefore, it is said that mountains, rivers, and the great earth are entirely the wondrously luminous true nature."

This is the "ear of the reflected image. Because the green waters and the vast sky manifest the *dharmakāya*, this interpretation combines the perspective of the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* (Characteristics of Phenomena) school.
If one were to interpret it solely according to the *Dharmatā* (Nature of Reality) school, Maitreya’s verse states:

"The essence of the conditioned is distinguished; to prevent that [misconception], three aspects are established. Because they differ from the essence, they are detached. That is the Tathāgata," referring to all conditioned phenomena.
Within this [Middle Way], the four characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing do not occur.

Therefore, when Bodhisattvas practice the contemplation of the Middle Way and seek the Buddha’s true, pure Dharma-body, they fear falling into the conditioned conceptualizations of the four characteristics of arising and ceasing.

Thus it is said: "To be apart from those is the Tathāgata. This refers to the previously cultivated sublime cause of detachment from characteristics; now, when the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) is exhausted, it is—
This serves to establish that the fruit is indeed devoid of marks.

△ Second, the fourfold section on severing doubts regarding the profundity and difficulty of believing in both cause and fruit. First, doubt due to a lack of faith; second, refuting doubt to reveal faith;
third, a detailed examination of the causes for faith; fourth, concluding by returning to the state devoid of marks. Now, first: doubt due to a lack of faith (this doubt...).
[This arises from] the two sections of the sūtra’s meaning: practicing giving without dwelling and seeing the Buddha without signs.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One... [up to] ...will they give rise to true faith in these spoken chapters and verses?”
Commentary: Master Zongle said: "Practicing giving without dwelling on signs is profound in terms of the cause; seeing the Buddha without marks is profound in terms of the fruit.
Since the dharma of cause and fruit is thus profound, those sentient beings with dull faculties who are currently deluded find it difficult to comprehend and cannot give rise to such genuine faith.
Fearing that there might be those who lack the necessary capacity, the Venerable One [the author] has composed this.
He addressed the Buddha and requested that he interrogate him. II. Dispelling Doubt and Revealing Faith:
The Buddha told Subhūti, "Do not speak thus... [until] ...one can give rise to faith and take this as real."

Commentary: Master Zongle said: "The Buddha’s answer indicates that not only do those with faith exist in the present, but in the future, at the end of the age, there will naturally be those endowed with merit and wisdom who, upon hearing this Prajñāpāramitā, can give rise to true faith. Regarding the "latter five hundred years," the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* states:
"The True Dharma lasts for one thousand years; these consist of two periods of five hundred years each. During the first five hundred years, one constantly cultivates liberation."
Because the precepts of meditation are firm, there follows a period of one thousand years of the Semblance Dharma (Sāṃketika-dharma), which also consists of two periods of five hundred years;

this is because learning and the cultivation of merit are firm. Third is the period of the Final Dharma (Paścima-dharma) for ten thousand years; regarding the first five hundred years, there is much that is false and contentious, because strife is firm;
they do not cultivate the precepts or meditative concentration, being largely greedy for gain and offerings, and mostly extremely indolent.
Because they are indolent, they strive for fame and seize profit in their actions; how much more so for those who hear the True Dharma and cultivate it?

Now the Buddha shows the Venerable One that even at the beginning of the ten-thousand-year period of this final age, there are still those with past roots of virtue who possess deep faith, let alone during the present and the two intermediate periods of the Right and Semblance Dharma.
Furthermore, "upholding" refers to the precepts; one must cultivate them.
Blessing (*puṇya*) is concentration (*samādhi*). Hearing the chapters and truly believing them is wisdom (*prajñā*). Thus, the verse of Maitreya says:
"To explain the profound meaning of cause and effect during that evil age is not in vain, for it possesses reality; the Bodhisattva is thus endowed with the three virtues.

These three virtues refer to the possession of the three trainings (*śikṣā*) of precepts, concentration, and wisdom. Therefore, we know that the Dharma does not obstruct faith, and time does not obstruct the capacity [of the recipient].
△ Third, the detailed explanation of the causes for faith has two parts: first, the roots of goodness are deep and far-reaching; second, wisdom and merit are perfected.
Regarding the first, that the roots of goodness are deep and far-reaching:
it should be known that such a person is not one who has produced pure faith in only one Buddha or two Buddhas (and so forth), nor even for a single moment of thought.
Zongle said: "If one discusses the source of genuine faith, it arises from having planted roots of goodness under many Buddhas;

thus, upon hearing this Mahāyāna Dharma, one is able to give rise to genuine faith. Even the arising of faith for a brief moment or a single thought likewise occurs because of the various roots of goodness planted under the Buddhas.
This is what is meant by saying that it is not until the stage of the ten levels of faith is fulfilled that one is [truly] supported."
The "Preparatory Practice for Provisions" refers to advancing to the stage of penetration (*prativedha*). Question: Why is it called "a single thought of true faith"? Answer:

It is because the direct mind and right mindfulness accord with the reality-body (*dharmatā*) of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Upon encountering objects, there is no arising; meeting conditions, one remains unmoved.

One realizes that birth and extinction are fundamentally without birth or extinction, does not fall into the realm of emotional consciousness, and stills the mind to reach the fundamental source. II. The Perfect Endowment of Merit and Wisdom.
Second: First, the Buddha’s wisdom clearly reflects all; second, the abandonment of attachment to self and phenomena. Now, regarding the first—Buddha’s wisdom clearly reflecting all:
Subhūti, the Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees that these sentient beings shall obtain such immeasurable merit.
Commentary: When the mind of faith arises for even a single thought-moment, all Buddhas know it completely.

Should any sentient being hear these phrases and develop even a single moment of pure faith, the Buddha’s eye of wisdom—perfect and all-illuminating—will clearly reflect their awakening to the wondrous, perfect, and fundamental nature.
They shall attain progress and penetration, roaming through the fruits of the ten stages until the state of perfection is reached; therefore, the merit obtained is immeasurable. △

Second, the abandonment of the two attachments to self and dharmas. First, the elimination of the attachment to the two extremes; second, the subsequent refutation of the reasons for the two views. Now, first, the elimination of the attachment to the two extremes. Why is this?
Because these sentient beings no longer possess the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span (*jīva*) (the emptiness of persons).
[One] sees that there is no mark of dharmas (which is the emptiness of dharmas), nor is there any mark of non-dharmas (further eliminating the view of signlessness).

Zongle says: This is an exegesis in accordance with the reason why generating faith results in the acquisition of merit; it encompasses both the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of dharmas. The Treatise states:

"Those who possess wisdom clearly understand the two kinds of selflessness—of persons and of dharmas"—therefore it is said that there are no longer [the notions of] self, person, multitude, or assembly.
The four marks of a living being give rise to the notion of a self; this is the emptiness of birth.

To say that there is neither the mark of dharmas nor the mark of non-dharmas is to sweep away the dualistic views of existence and non-existence. △ Second, the reason for turning back to refute these two views.
Why is this? Because if these sentient beings take signs with their minds (up to the point where they) become attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
Zongle says: This reveals that violating the sutra results in a lack of merit. To say "taking signs with the mind" and so forth refers to the view of self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*).
Now, because the view of self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*) has been shattered, the mind does not grasp at signs or conceptions.

If one were to grasp at the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), this would be the view of clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). If one does not grasp [at them], then even the view of clinging to phenomena becomes empty. Why is this?

If one were to grasp at what is non-dharmic and so forth, it would be said that although the Great Being is empty of the two views of self and phenomena, he has destroyed their marks and extinguished his mind; furthermore, there is the fear of being bitten.

O Āyuṣmat, having fallen into the pit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), you are unable to transcend it; how could the Dharma of the Mind-Seal of the Middle Way possibly attain perfect and wondrous merit?
△ Fourth, the conclusion returning to the signless.
"Therefore, one should not grasp at dharmas, nor should one grasp at non-dharmas" (up to) "even dharmas should be relinquished, how much more so non-dharmas.

Regarding the "full explanation": one should not grasp at the mind, nor should one grasp at dharmas and so forth. This means that internally, one does not grasp at the mind, because when seeking the mind, it is ultimately unobtainable.
Externally, one does not grasp at the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), because one realizes that objects are fundamentally empty.

Since contact with objects is non-arising and is neither arising nor ceasing, one should not grasp at what is non-dharma, for fear that the great beings (*mahāsattva*) of initial resolve might enter *parinirvāṇa*.

"Furthermore," [it means: once the mind and its objects have been eliminated, what dharma is there to be cultivated or realized? Therefore, although one perceives the unconditioned reality (*asaṃskṛta-bhūtakoṭi*), one does not abide in the perception of the unconditioned.

Thus it is said that "one should not grasp at non-dharmas. Regarding the phrase "for this reason, etc.," it means that the Buddha is ever...
I demonstrate this to the assembly of bhikṣus: I constantly manifest both existence and non-existence in order to sweep away the clinging views of sentient beings.
You must not follow my words and letters to turn toward views that grasp at existence, grasp at non-existence, or grasp at that which is neither existent nor non-existent.
I constantly teach and demonstrate like a person crossing with a raft; do not give rise to views or conceptualizations regarding language and letters. Furthermore...

It is like using a finger to point at the moon; do not mistake the finger for the moon. It is merely a matter of using something other than a tree, such as the wind moving or a fan, to indicate the moon.

As for the statement, "Even dharmas should be relinquished, how much more so non-dharmas," this means that even the Dharma of the Mind-Seal of the True Mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) should be relinquished and not grasped through views, let alone grasping the view of annihilationism regarding non-dharmas. It is as ungraspable as it is pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, reaching everywhere in its perfection. Wisdom is ungraspable, yet its functional application is fully manifest within the mind and eyes.

"Subhūti, what do you think? [up to] "Therefore, the Tathāgata says that the merit is great.

Therefore, the verse says: "Only the Buddhas' Dharma brings about the supreme essence of merit. Furthermore, the Buddha feared that the Venerable One might become attached [to this].

The first is so called because it is free from contention (*araṇa*). In the Sanskrit language, it is *araṇa-vihāra*; in the Chinese language, it is "practice of non-contention" (*wuzhengxing*).

To be "without contention" means to be free from two kinds of hindrances: first, the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), which refers to the exhaustion of the delusions of views and thoughts; second, the hindrance to wisdom (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Thus, one does not calculate or grasp at the view of the nature of *nirvāṇa*; therefore, there is no contention.

If one were to say, "I have realized it for myself," one would fall into the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Because in reality there is nothing to be attained, one seals the realization of my own tranquility. 5.

Now, "non-apprehension" does not mean falling into the view of nihilism. As the *Mātṛkā-gāthā* of the *Vijñaptimātra* states:

"When the cognition of the object of apprehension has nothing to be apprehended, at that time one abides in *vijñaptimātra*, because one is free from the characteristics of the two graspings. Now, as for being free from the two graspings:

One attains the true ultimate nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*). Therefore, phenomena cannot be said to exist or not to exist; one first realizes the limit of non-arising (*anutpatti-pada*).
△ Sixth: Severing the doubt that the adornment of the land contradicts non-appropriation (this doubt also arises from the third doubt regarding "ungraspability").
"Subhūti, what do you think? [up to] "one should generate the mind without abiding anywhere.
Commentary: The intent of the doubt is this: since dharmas are not ultimately graspable, how can the bodhisattvas cultivate the myriad practices and yet still grasp a pure land?
Fearing that such a doubt might arise, the Buddha counters by asking a question in order to interrogate him, saying: "The Bodhisattva adorns the Buddha..."
The Buddha questioned him once more. The Venerable One immediately grasped the Buddha’s intention and said: "That which adorns the Buddha-lands is not adornment; it is merely called adornment.
Now, the cultivation of the sublime practices of the six perfections is fundamentally free from all marks (*nimitta*).
It dissolves back into the true ultimate nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), which is inherently pure. Therefore, it is said: "According as the mind is pure, so is the Buddha."

The earth is pure. Therefore, when it is said that "all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind," this is a warning to the beginner Bodhisattva that one must by no means fall into the realm of sounds and forms.

Consequently, one should not abide in the objective shadows of the six sense-objects, such as form and so forth; rather, one should give rise to the mind by abiding nowhere. As for the giving rise to the mind:
This means that with a mind that dwells nowhere, one practices the perfections such as generosity moment by moment;

because one realizes moment by moment that the characteristics of the perfections such as generosity are unattainable, and through this unattainability, the characteristics of arising and ceasing are themselves without arising or ceasing—there is only True Suchness (tathatā).
This is what is called severing hindrances and realizing the truth, like the moon on the fifteenth night, gradually becoming full and radiant.

The following text states: "When the mind of faith is pure, one gives birth to the true aspect (*dharmatā*). Upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood, the true aspect is partially realized and finally perfected;
this is what is meant by 'giving birth to the mind. The verse says: 'Wisdom practices the nature of consciousness-only; thus one takes up the Pure Land.

"Is this not great? The Venerable One immediately and deeply realized the Buddha’s intent, saying: "It is said that all Bodhisattvas transform consciousness into wisdom and attain untainted conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*).
They suddenly empty both the two dharmas of form and mind, and definitively lack any self-grasping through conceptual discrimination.

Now that I have attained the realization of the fruit of the Reward Body (*sambhoga-kāya*), if there were even for a single moment a mind characterized by self-grasping, I would immediately fall back into the limits of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)."
The limits of measurement can never be identical with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Because one does not grasp [at them], they become identical with the limit of reality;
therefore, the Venerable One replied, "It is exceedingly great. It is just like Sumeru, the king of mountains, which stands within the world as the highest and greatest.

Because one ultimately does not grasp at self-characteristics (svalakṣaṇa). It is the same for the Bodhisattva: when attaining the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya), one never says that they have personally realized it.
This is because there is no characteristic of a self-body; since there is no attainment, it is called attainment, and since there is no reception, it is called reception.
Because it is free from all characteristics, it is identical to the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and equal to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); therefore, it is said to be "the Buddha’s teaching."
That which is not a body is called the "Great Body. Thus, a verse by Maitreya says: "Like the King of Mountains, it is without grasping;

its reception of retribution is likewise so, for it is far removed from all outflows (*āsrava*) and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). It further states: "One realizes the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)."
That which is not a body is the Great Body. Now, as for the Bodhi of the Buddha: it is the stilling of the mind to reach the fundamental source, wherein all myriad concerns are utterly discarded.
