Because that which is observed is itself cessation, one ceases while observing; because there is no observation apart from observation, one observes while ceasing.

Furthermore, since observation is fundamentally cessation and cessation is fundamentally observation, stillness and contemplation are fused as a pair. Through wondrous concentration, it is itself wisdom;
through wondrous wisdom, it is itself concentration. Only then is True Suchness (Tathatā) vibrantly active, suddenly entering the gold.
This concludes the method for the Mind-Seal of Firmness. The first section, the Exposition of the Main Body (*śarīra*), is hereby completed. △ Third is the Section on Circulation (*pariṇāmanā*).
After the Buddha had spoken this sutra, from "the Elder Subhūti" [up to] "all were greatly rejoiced, and they believed, accepted, and practiced it."
Commentary: "When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra" refers to the conclusion of the exposition on the meaning of Prajñā within the Dharma-treasury compiled by Ānanda;
it is a phrase used to mark the end of the discourse. "The Elder Subhūti" identifies the foremost among those who requested the Dharma.

The two characters for *bhikṣu* have already been explained previously. *Śramaṇerī* is a Sanskrit term translated here as "nun. The preceding mention of "bhikṣus and so forth" [is as previously detailed].
The two groups of those who have left the household life refer to the monks and nuns. The later "upāsakas and upāsikās" refer to the two groups of householders.
The terms *upāsaka* and *upāsikā* are Sanskrit; in this [language], they are translated as "male lay devotee" (*jìnshì nán*) and "female lay devotee" (*jìnshì nǚ*).
As for the term "lay devotee" (*jìnshì*), it means that the two groups of householders fully receive the five precepts and constantly attend upon and make offerings to [the Sangha].
The Three Jewels constitute their primary task. Therefore, the two assemblies of the laity are called the "external protectors" of the Three Jewels;

they propagate the True Dharma and universally lead sentient beings of various kinds into the Buddha-way. Thus, the two assemblies of those who have left the home life are called the "internal protectors" of the Three Jewels;
they expound the Dharma to benefit living beings and gather all multitudes, universally rescuing and guiding them through the three vehicles.
Because they lead those lost in the deluded ways into nirvāṇa. Now, among the four classes of the Buddha’s disciples, only the bhikṣu serves as their leader.

Furthermore, from among these bhikṣus, one must select those who possess the requisite equipment and virtue; only then may [the teaching] be transmitted. These are: first, having attained the Dharma-eye;
second, possessing the virtue of the precepts; third, being endowed with meditative concentration and wisdom; fourth, possessing eloquence; fifth...

First, they possess the faculties of the Mahāyāna; second, they possess the nature of great compassion; third, they possess the perfection of the marks and signs of a Buddha; fourth, they possess the perfection of merit; fifth, they possess the perfection of wisdom;

sixth, they possess the nature of great compassion; and seventh, they possess the perfection of the qualities of voice and appearance. If one lacks even one or two of these virtues, it is difficult for them to serve as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*);

how then could they transmit the lineage and sustain the life of wisdom? If, indeed, they possess these seven virtues, they shall traverse the dharma-gate of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), or [attain] the ancient...
This is the Buddha’s repeated manifestation. That which is called the unceasing circulation of the Dharma pervades the *sāhasra-lokadhātu*;
how could it be measured? Regarding the phrase "all worlds" and so forth: "Heaven" refers to the twenty-eight heavens of the triple realm; "human" [refers to the human world].
This refers to those from the sons of heaven down to the common people. "Asura" is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "Non-God.
They possess the blessings of gods but lack the virtues of gods, as explained in detail elsewhere. The word "etc.

(等) includes various other classes of beings, such as the world of vessels (*bhājanaloka*) and the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Upon hearing that the Buddha had arrived...
Those who believe, accept, and practice—whosoever is within the assembly of Prajñā—hears the Buddha’s intent at once:

namely, that by sweeping away form and emptiness one transcends existence, and by cleansing the eyes of ordinary and sage one enters the single mind. Thus, one penetrates the fundamental source of the Dharma-realm and realizes the great awakening of perfect luminosity.
How could it not be that they all experience great joy, believing and accepting this, and swiftly attain the severance of hindrances and the realization of the Truth?
O practitioners! The verse of dedication says:
By the power of my diligence, And with a wondrous mind moved by compassion and wisdom, I have used the ordinary intellect of the hair-path to measure the emptiness of the Dharma-realm;
Without grasping at the limits of nature or characteristics, Through wondrous contemplation, I enter the unconditioned.
Transcending the practices of the ten stages, he has eternally realized the fruit of permanence and bliss.
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (End).
Phonetic Glossary.

Commentary: To understand that the phenomena of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are fundamentally quiescent and extinguished—namely, the category of the five aggregates, the category of the twelve bases, and the category of the eighteen elements—the term *skandha* in Sanskrit is translated into Chinese as "accumulation" (*yùn*). The *Renwang jing* states:
"All sentient beings possess two types of phenomena: form and mind. Form is called the aggregate of form; mind is called the four [mental] aggregates. All are accumulations."

The "aggregates" (skandhas) conceal the true nature; they are the five aggregates of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. This constitutes the "theory of unifying form and opening the mind.

Second, regarding the twelve bases (āyatanas): the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and the objects of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch are called the ten bases of material phenomena (rūpa-dharma).
Furthermore, these two bases [the mind and mental objects] constitute the "dharma-objects," which are the objects of the sixth consciousness and the seventh consciousness respectively.

There is a half-portion, namely: the "solitary shadow" object (*kevala-chāyā-viṣaya*), as well as the "true substantial" (*sat-pratibimba*) and "apparent substantial" (*pratibimba-sadṛśa*) objects discussed in the treatise;

this refers specifically to non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*). As for "mind," it refers to the six consciousnesses and the "seeing portion" (*darśana-bhāga*) of the mental consciousness discussed in the treatise;

this is what is meant by the "treatise that opens up matter and combines mind. Regarding the "thirty-eight elements" (*dhātu*): these refer to the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses, which constitute ten [elements].
The eight elements (*dhātu*). As for "elements," each has its own boundary; this constitutes the discourse on both mind and matter being opened up.

The first five aggregates (*skandha*) are substantial; within the elements and bases (*āyatana*), they are provisional. This is the meaning of the three categories (*tri-dharmaskandha*) according to the discourse on the provisional and the real.

If one traces back the stream to its source, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is formed due to delusion regarding the wisdom of self-nature; this is the discourse on whether it is more or less [substantial]. It is formed due to delusion regarding nature.

Regarding form (*rūpa*), there is also the discourse on "more" or "less. If one can transform consciousness (*vijñāna*) into wisdom (*jñāna*), then the nature [of phenomena] is transformed such that one no longer calculates [them as] self, person, or other dharmas.

By means of wisdom, one comprehends form; because form is like a reflection and cannot be apprehended, the nature [of form] merges with wisdom. Since wisdom cannot be apprehended, the nature of wisdom and [the nature of form] are of one suchness.
This is what is called the sense-base of touch becoming the true Dharma; all dharmas are fundamentally and eternally quiescent.
Because it is extinguished, this is the Mind-Seal (*cittamudrā*). The Commentary states:

"By severing the ten obstructions and realizing the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*), one exhausts the source; through the diamond-like wisdom (*vajrajñāna*) of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), one reaches the other shore.
The Sub-commentary notes: "The ten obstructions are the innate cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the ten stages (*bhūmi*). As for the ten suchnesses:"

This refers to the *tathatā* (suchness) realized within the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Here, they are termed the "ten obstacles. First is the obstacle of the ordinary person’s mark of self (*pṛthagjana-ātma-nimitta-āvaraṇa*), which consists of two types of ignorance (*moha*):
first, the ignorance of clinging to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-abhiniveśa-moha*), which is the obstacle of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-āvaraṇa*);

second, the ignorance of defilement in the evil destinies (*durgati-saṃkleśa-moha*), which refers to the various karmas and fruits of the evil destinies. Although these karmas and fruits are not themselves of the nature of ignorance, they are categorized as such because they belong to the same class as ignorance.
Therefore, if one eliminates this single hindrance and its two delusions, one immediately realizes the universally pervasive true thusness (*sarvatraga-tathatā*).
This is because the two kinds of emptiness manifested by this true thusness are such that there is not a single dharma that does not exist therein. Once this true thusness has been realized...
One immediately enters the Bodhisattva’s first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

It is called "Joy" because, having for the first time attained the noble nature (*ārya-dharma*) and fully realized the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), one is able to benefit oneself and others, thereby giving rise to great joy. Furthermore, there are three meanings:

first, attaining the stage; second, realizing the principle; and third, accomplishing the practice. Because of these three, it is named "Supreme Joy. This is the initial realization of a portion of reality.

Because the wisdom of the *lakṣaṇa-vajra* has reached the further shore (*pāramitā*). Second is the obstacle of false views. This refers to the obstacles of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind committed through error.
These obstacles consist of two types of delusion: first, the delusion of subtle transgressions; second, the delusion regarding the various courses of karma.
By means of this one hindrance and two delusions, the second stage is obstructed.

If one eliminates this one hindrance and two delusions, one realizes the most excellent *tathatā* (suchness) and fully accomplishes the virtue of boundless pure precepts; for it is the most supreme among all phenomena.
Once this *tathatā* has been realized, one enters the Bodhisattva’s second stage, the Stainless (*vimalā*). Thus it is said.

"Free from defilement" (vimalā) means that one is utterly remote from the defilement of transgressing the precepts; that is, one is endowed with natural morality (*prakṛti-śīla*), rather than the morality attained through deliberation as on the first stage.

For this reason, it is called the Stage Free from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*). Furthermore, by progressing further, one realizes the second portion—the perfection of the vajra-like wisdom of the true nature (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*)—thereby reaching the other shore.
The three obstacles of dullness and rigidity immediately cause [the cessation of] hearing and reflection.

The cultivation of the three types of wisdom is forgotten, and there are obstacles to superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and dhāraṇī. Because these obstacles consist of two kinds of ignorance:

first, the ignorance of desire, which obstructs superior meditative concentration and the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*); second, the ignorance regarding the perfection of dhāraṇī, which obstructs the wisdom of hearing (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*), as well as the dhāraṇī itself.
If one eliminates this single obstacle and its two types of ignorance, one immediately realizes the superior [attainment].
The "flowing True Suchness" refers to the teachings that flow forth from this True Suchness, for they are exceedingly supreme.
Once one has realized this True Suchness, one enters the third bodhisattva stage, the Luminous (Prabhākari).

It is called the Luminous Stage because, through the accomplishment of superior meditative concentrations and dhāraṇīs, one gives rise to the light of boundless, wondrous wisdom. Furthermore, one proceeds...
Because one has reached the perfection of the vajra-wisdom that thoroughly realizes the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the third stage;

[the fourth is] the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle afflictions, namely, the non-abandonment of attachment to meditative concentration (*samādhi-rāga*) and attachment to the Dharma (*dharma-rāga*). This obstacle consists of two types of ignorance.
First, there is the delusion of savoring the eight meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). Second, there is the delusion of craving for dharmas, which is the pride of understanding the Dharma.

Since one has now attained untainted meditative absorption and untainted wisdom through the teachings, this [delusion] is contradicted. By severing these two obstacles and two delusions, one realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) that is free from grasping;
having done so, one immediately accomplishes the bodhi-dharma of the non-abiding path, proceeding with diligence and without regression.

One attains entry into the fourth Bodhisattva stage, the Stage of Pervasive Wisdom (*prabhākarī-bhūmi*). Regarding the term "Flaming Wisdom" (*jvalanaprabhā*), it is a name that manifests both through its literal meaning and its metaphorical significance, and it possesses three meanings:
first, the initial realization of wisdom is able to burn away the fuel of pride regarding the understanding of phenomena belonging to the preceding stage;
second, by abiding in the most excellent Dharma of Bodhi, the flames of wisdom increase as they burn away the fuel of afflictions; and third, because the third stage has been brought to fulfillment.
It is called "Blazing Wisdom" (*Arciṣmatī*) because it emits the light of pure wisdom from the jewel of realized knowledge; for these three reasons, it is named the Ground of Blazing Wisdom.
Furthermore, it is so called because one advances to exhaustively realize the fourth part of the true nature (*dharmatā*), reaching the perfection of adamantine wisdom (*vajra-jñāna*).

Fifth is the obstacle to the nirvāṇa of the inferior vehicles (*hīnayāna*). This refers to the obstacle in the preceding four stages (*bhūmi*) where one seeks nirvāṇa out of world-transcending revulsion for the suffering of birth and death.
This obstacle consists of two delusions: first, longing; second, aversion. That is to say, it is the longing for the tranquility of nirvāṇa and the aversion toward the suffering of saṃsāra.
Because these two obstacles exist, it is difficult to transcend them, and thus one has not yet attained [the higher stages] of the Two Vehicles.

Emerging from the ultimate and entering the conventional for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, by severing this single hindrance and two types of ignorance, one realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) that is undifferentiated in its categories;
that is to say, this *tathatā* is equal in both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Once this *tathatā* has been realized, one enters the fifth bodhisattva stage, the "Difficult to Conquer" (*sudurjayā*). As for the term "Difficult to Conquer," it is because...
The knowledge of ultimate truth within the ground is non-conceptual, whereas the worldly knowledge of crafts is conceptual.

Since these two truths—ultimate and conventional—are contradictory, one must cause them to be joined; because it is difficult to join what is not easily joined yet succeeds in joining them, and because they are brought into extreme correspondence, it is called the "Difficult to Conquer" ground (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, one advances to fully realize the fifth portion of the reality-mark (*dharmatā*) through adamantine wisdom (*vajra-jñāna*).

Because of reaching the other shore. The sixth is the obstacle of the manifestation of coarse characteristics; that is, because of the manifestation of coarse characteristics consisting of grasping at defilement and purity.
This obstacle consists of two types of ignorance: first, ignorance regarding the flow of the modes of activity, which is the grasping at defilement herein;
second, ignorance regarding the manifestation of manifold characteristics, which is the grasping at purity herein. If...
By severing this single hindrance and its two delusions, one realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) that is inherently undefiled and pure.
This means that the intrinsic nature of this *tathatā* is originally free from defilement and cannot be said to become pure only later.

Once this *tathatā* is realized, one enters the sixth Bodhisattva stage, the Stage of Manifestation (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*). Regarding the term "manifestation," the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra* states: "It does not abide in birth..."
Regarding "death and nirvāṇa": because the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) manifests before one, it is called the "Manifesting Ground" (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*).

Furthermore, because one advances to exhaustively realize the sixth division—the diamond-like wisdom of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*)—and thereby reaches the further shore (*pāramitā*), it is so named. The obstacle of the active manifestation of the seven subtle marks consists in the active manifestation of the subtle marks of arising and ceasing;
this mark of arising and ceasing constitutes two types of delusion: first, the active manifestation of subtle marks.

The first is the delusion of clinging to the existence of subtle rebirth within the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*). The second is the delusion of exclusively seeking the signless (*animitta*) through mental attention, which is the clinging to the existence of subtle cessation (*nivṛtti*).
If one eliminates this single obstacle and these two delusions, one realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) that is undifferentiated from all phenomena;
for by understanding the various teachings, they become darkly identical with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Once this *tathatā* has been realized, [one attains the fruit].
One immediately enters the seventh Bodhisattva stage, the *Dūraṅgamā-bhūmi* (The Far-Reaching). Regarding the term "far-reaching," the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"Because it is far from the triple world (*tridhātu*) and near to the station of the Dharma King, it is named the Far-Reaching Stage. Furthermore, because one advances to the ultimate realization of the seventh-part true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), attaining the adamantine wisdom (*vajra-jñāna*) that reaches the other shore, it is so called.
This is the obstacle to the unconditioned practice (*animitta-prayoga*) within the signless (*animitta*). Specifically, within the signless—

Because there is still further application of effort (*prayoga*), one is as yet unable to manifest the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and the land (*kṣetra*). This obstruction consists of two types of ignorance (*moha*):

first, ignorance regarding the effortful application toward the signless (*animitta*); second, ignorance regarding mastery over mental images (*saṃjñā-vaśitā*), which prevents one from attaining mastery over the marks.
By abandoning this single hindrance and its two types of delusion, one realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) that is neither increasing nor decreasing;

that is to say, because this *tathatā* does not follow along with defilement or purity, nor with increase or decrease. Once this *tathatā* has been realized, one enters the eighth bodhisattva stage, the Immovable (*acalā*).
It is called "immovable" because non-conceptual wisdom flows on spontaneously and uninterruptedly. Its characteristics are as follows:

It is called the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*) because one is unshakable by afflictions. Furthermore, it is so named because one advances to the ultimate realization of the eighth stage—the *vajra-jñāna* of the true nature (*dharmatā*)—and thereby reaches the further shore.
Regarding the ninth [stage], there is the obstacle of not wishing to act for the benefit of others;

this consists of two delusions (*moha*) resulting from the obstacles to the four types of unhindered knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*). The first is the delusion regarding the names, phrases, and syllables of the infinite teachings of the Dharma.

Subsequently, there is the delusion regarding mastery over dhāraṇīs and wisdom, and secondly, the delusion regarding mastery over eloquence; this is precisely the obstacle to the fourth unimpeded knowledge, that of analytical exposition (*pratibhāna*).
If one eliminates these two delusions and this single obstacle, one realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) that serves as the basis for mastery over gnosis (*jñāna-vaśitā*).
That is to say, once this *tathatā* has been realized, one enters the ninth bodhisattva stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*). Thus it is said.
Regarding "Good Intelligence" (*Sādhumatī*): because one attains the most excellent unimpeded wisdom (*anāvaraṇa-jñāna*), it is named the Stage of Good Intelligence.

Furthermore, because one advances to the ultimate realization of the ninth part—the diamond-like wisdom of the true nature of reality (*dharmatā-tathatā*)—and reaches the other shore, there is the tenth obstacle: the obstacle to mastery over phenomena (*dharma-vaśitā*).

This is precisely the obstacle to the great cloud of dharma-wisdom (*mahā-dharma-jñāna-megha*) of the tenth stage and the activities (*karma*) arising therefrom. Within this single obstacle, there are...

There are two delusions: first, the delusion regarding supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) that arises from obstacles; second, the delusion regarding great wisdom, which is the inability to penetrate subtle secrets.
If one eliminates these two delusions and their corresponding obstacles, one realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) that serves as the basis for mastery over karma.
This means that this *tathatā* possesses the gates of dhāraṇī and samādhi, as well as the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) pertaining to the reception of the [Bodhisattva] rank.
Because it conceals all secret activities. Once this *tathatā* (suchness) has been realized, one enters the tenth bodhisattva stage, the Dharma-Cloud (*dharmameghā*).
Regarding the "Dharma-Cloud": it refers to the *dharmakāya*, which is like space; its wisdom is like a great cloud.
Furthermore, by means of the various gates of bodhisattva samādhis and dhāraṇīs, it gathers all causes perfumed by hearing and pervades the Tathāgata.

Within the *Treatise on the Ten Stages* (*Daśabhūmika-śāstra*), it is said that by means of these clouds of perfuming through hearing, one causes a great rain of Dharma to fall throughout the entire dharma-realm, sufficing immeasurable sentient beings;

this is called the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*Dharmameghā-bhūmi*). Furthermore, as one advances to exhaustively realize the tenth stage’s ultimate reality (*dharmatā*), it is said that "one severs the ten obstacles and realizes the ten suchnesses.
Thus, through investigating and exhausting the truth until the ultimate realization of the reality-mark (*lakṣaṇa*) is attained, one reaches that state via vajra-like wisdom.
Because they are the "banks. Furthermore, these ten hindrances do not transcend the four marks of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing found in the *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra*.
As for the four marks, they are arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. As for the three subtleties, they are: first, the mark of karma; second, the mark of transformation;
and third, the mark of manifestation. As for the six coarsenesses, they are: first, the mark of cognition; second, the mark of continuity; and third, the mark of grasping.
Fourth is the characteristic of names; fifth is the characteristic of performing karma; sixth is the characteristic of the fruit of suffering bound by karma.

Within these three subtle and six coarse characteristics, none transcend the phases of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. These are severed through the three stages of worthiness, the ten bhūmis, and the two types of sublime awakening.
This refers to the fact that both those prior to the stages (bhūmi) and the śrāvakas of the small fruit have equally severed the two characteristics of differentiation. Why is this?

Because by advancing from the stage of the worthy (ārya) to the first bhūmi, one destroys the grasping at the characteristic of names within the sixth and seventh consciousnesses; therefore, [the nature of] the sixth and seventh consciousnesses...
Furthermore, regarding the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, one forever abandons the dualistic grasping of discrimination;

one resolutely does not create them. Therefore, prior to the [first] bhūmi, one destroys the two marks of difference. As for the śrāvakas of the four fruits: the first fruit (srotāpanna) destroys the ten kinds of view-afflictions within the sixth consciousness.
Having first abandoned the self and dharmas, they never again create karma and never again invite bitter fruits. Thus, this is the mark of cessation. Second.
Regarding the three or four fruits: because it destroys the seventh *pravṛtti-vijñāna* and serves as the root for the sixth *manovijñāna*, it is called the "mind-root" (*manas-indriya*).
This seventh consciousness constantly and thoroughly deliberates, following along with the notion of a self.

Because it relies on the six consciousnesses to discriminate between the objects of the sensory realms—whether good or evil—it grasps at names and designations, giving rise to afflictions, creating karma, and inviting karmic results.

Now, as the sixth consciousness moment by moment cultivates morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, it causes the seventh consciousness to likewise accomplish morality, concentration, and so forth, moment by moment.
This breaks the attachment to the grasping of names and the self and phenomena, which is the characteristic of divergent views.
Furthermore, it causes the active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) arising from the sixth and seventh consciousnesses to permeate and enter the eighth consciousness.

Within this, the seeds of the self-view and its associated dharmas are likewise entirely uprooted. Thus, one destroys the seeds of the nine grades of afflictions of thought within the seventh consciousness of the desire realm.

Furthermore, when Śrāvakas cultivate untainted concentration and wisdom, they take the nature of the ālayavijñāna as their object within the seventh consciousness, permanently relinquishing all calculation of it as a self;
they then [uproot] the ignorance of self, the pride of self, and the view of self within the eighth consciousness.

I cherish the four delusions; therefore, by utterly uprooting the most subtle seeds of the self and dharmas, I suddenly sever the seventy-two grades of afflictions of the outflows (*āsrava-kleśa*) pertaining to the realms of form and formlessness. There are two ways to destroy these afflictions of the outflows.
First, because ordinary beings savor the eight meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the form and formless realms, they create obstacles to the fruits of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).

Consequently, they have not yet escaped *paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa* (segmented birth and death) and, upon the exhaustion of their retribution, return to the cycle of rebirths. Now, the Arhat does not savor or grasp these;
having forever abandoned the flavor of meditative absorption, this is called the "eight liberations" (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*). Second, it is because he does not reckon the nature of the *ālayavijñāna*.

They forever abandon my Dharma, suddenly severing the delusions of self-view and craving; they do not even calculate or grasp at nirvāṇa, let alone calculate or grasp at the nature of the ālayavijñāna.
Thus, they forever abandon birth and death and do not follow saṃsāra, achieving the fruit of the "slayer of the thief" which is non-arising.

The non-Buddhists, however, due to calculating the flavor of meditative absorption and calculating the nature of consciousness, falsely grasp at the view of the nature of nirvāṇa and falsely realize it.
Because there is no birth, the seeds of those who act as thieves to my Dharma have never been entirely eradicated; how could they ever transcend birth and death? Question:
The followers of the Hīnayāna previously did not know that the eighth consciousness exists; why then do you now say that the eighth consciousness exists? Answer:

Although the followers of the Hīnayāna do not know it exists, the habitual seeds of the afflictions of the fragmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*) that they sever are all contained within the eight consciousnesses.

[This] is severed. If one in the stage of the noble ones prior to the [ten] stages enters into penetration and attains a portion of the path of seeing, this is also equal to the vision of the stage of an Arhat;
however, the Arhat does not yet know that there are no phenomena external to the mind, and that things arise in their very place and are extinguished in their very place.
It is indestructible; it is solely this one mind. By realizing the Great Non-arising, one accomplishes the fruit of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

If an Arhat is able to know and comprehend this, suddenly emptying the self-nature of both form and mind so that they are perfectly luminous, he immediately transcends all stages and attains entry into the Non-arising.
Furthermore, regarding the severance of the ignorance of abiding in signs: this refers to abandoning the state of an ordinary being at the First Stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*).

Following the obstacles, until one reaches the sixth stage, the *Abhimukhī-bhūmi*, the dualistic arising and ceasing of both defiled and purified appearances continues to flow and turn, never having been fully escaped or exhausted.
Only when one has entered the sixth stage can the coarse arising and ceasing of appearances be permanently abandoned through their active manifestation;

therefore, among the characteristics of abiding, this refers to the characteristic of continuity (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, while the Bodhisattva is in the sixth stage and has not yet entered the seventh...

At the stage of the Grounds (*bhūmi*), there still remains the wisdom of the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*) that has not yet been fully liberated; therefore, while abiding within signs, the characteristics of wisdom have not yet been shattered.

Only upon entering the Seventh Ground is one able to sever them forever. Having first realized non-arising (*anutpāda*), the six coarse [defilements] are permanently abandoned, yet the three subtle [defilements] remain unremoved;
thus, one has not yet entered the Great Patience of Non-arising (*mahā-anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). At the Eighth Ground, one realizes and enters the Great...
The patience of birth (*janma-kṣānti*) suddenly shatters the manifest aspect within the eighth consciousness; that is to say, it is precisely the two aspects of "intimate" and "distant.

Furthermore, when one is about to enter the ninth stage from the eighth stage, the subtle self-clinging within the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness has not yet been completely abandoned.
Therefore, before advancing from the eighth stage to the ninth stage, the four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) have not yet been attained.

When one enters the eighth consciousness of the ninth stage (*bhūmi*), the evolving aspect of the *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-part) is finally and permanently abandoned, and one further realizes non-arising (*anutpāda*).

The two coarse aspects—namely, the subsequent wisdom (*anuparivartin-jñāna*) and the manifest transformation (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*)—constitute the ignorance of the abiding aspect (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*).

The subsequent seeds constitute the ignorance of the arising aspect (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*). Thus, it is called the "arising aspect" because it refers to both the seeing and the perceived aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*).

The subtle dual grasping of the *vibhāga* (discrimination) and *nimitta* (appearance) is assigned as the branches and leaves of ignorance (*avidyā*). The seeds of the two divisions of appearance and discrimination, along with the *karmalakṣaṇa* (karmic aspect), constitute the root ignorance.

Therefore, the three subtleties and six grossnesses are combined and assigned to the stages of the noble ones (*ārya*), corresponding to the four characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.
Furthermore, they are assigned to the five, six, seven, and eight consciousnesses and eliminated through their refutation, beginning with the entry into the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Regarding the stages of the path: even within the two types of enlightenment—the Equal and the Sublime—there remains the most subtle of the subtle seeds of the characteristics of karma and ignorance that have not yet been exhausted;
therefore, one has not yet realized the fruit-virtue of the ocean of sublime, perfect awakening. Question:

After the adamantine path, the fruit of maturation is empty; because seeds are both subject to arising and ceasing and not subject to arising and ceasing, one further distinguishes between the two stages of Equality and Wondrousness to sever them.
"Completely devoid of the characteristics of maturation (*vipāka*). The *Zongjing lu* states: "The eighth consciousness originally has no name of *ālaya*.

It is because the seventh consciousness clings to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth as a self that it is so designated. If this clinging were not maintained, it would simply be called the 'maturation consciousness' (*vipākavijñāna*).
This is the state of the fruit of good and evil; with good and evil karma as its cause, it is thus summoned and obtained."

This is the principle of cause and effect. Thus, the karma of previous lives serves as the cause; this cause being either wholesome or unwholesome, it brings forth in the present life the eighth consciousness, which is the neutral (avyākṛta) fruit of maturation (vipāka).

Because the characteristics of birth and death—both the segmented (paricchinna) and the transformational (pariṇāma) types, whether mundane or supramundane—cannot be fully exhausted, one proceeds until after the path of the diamond-like samādhi (vajropama-samādhi), when the fruit of maturation becomes empty. Thereupon, the ten obstacles are severed and realization is attained.
The ten suchnesses (tathatā) are utterly devoid of the characteristics of karmic maturation (vipāka). Like the solitary fullness of the moon in the mind, they are ultimately beyond verbal expression.

Thus, the eight consciousnesses are transformed into the four wisdoms (*jñāna*). (Note: The eight consciousnesses are: 1. eye-consciousness; 2. ear-consciousness; 3. nose-consciousness; 4. tongue-consciousness;
5. body-consciousness; 6. mental consciousness; 7. evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*); 8. storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). The four wisdoms are as follows:)
These are: first, the wisdom of accomplishment; second, the wisdom of wondrous observation; third, the wisdom of equality; and fourth, the great mirror-like wisdom.
It is said that the former two wisdoms predominantly take conventional truth as their object, while the latter two wisdoms predominantly take ultimate truth as their object.
What is called the transformation of the preceding five consciousnesses—eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—is the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
This means that while among ordinary beings, these consciousnesses were involved in the functioning of the sense organs and their objects—the five sensory realms of sound, form, and so forth;

now, in the stage of Buddhahood, they are able to respond and transform, manifesting according to the capacities of sentient beings even through bodies such as mountains and rivers. Therefore, it is called "Accomplishing What Is to Be Done."

Regarding wisdom: as for the transformation of the former sixth consciousness into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation, this means that while in the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), the sixth consciousness constantly and critically deliberates, capable of discerning the various objects of the five sensory realms through inference (*anumāna*).

Specifically, it does so by means of the "true semblance with a shared essence" (*sabhāga-sadṛśa-nimitta*). Now, in the stage of Buddhahood, this is transformed into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation.
The wisdom that discerns and reflects upon the differences among capacities and can teach the Dharma according to those faculties is called the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (wisdom of wondrous observation).
Regarding the transformation of the seventh consciousness prior to the three turnings into the *samatā-jñāna* (wisdom of equality):

while in the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), the seventh consciousness is originally named *manas*, which here means "discriminating consciousness" and is also called the "defiled-pure consciousness. It discriminates between existence and non-existence.
Because it gives rise to the appearance of defilement, it now transforms into the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*) within the state of Buddhahood.
It eternally severs the appearances of the two extremes and profoundly realizes the realm of the patience regarding non-arising and quiescence; therefore, it is named the Wisdom of Equality.

Regarding the transformation of the eighth consciousness into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*): this refers to its original name as the *ālayavijñāna* during the stage of an ordinary being.
Ālaya-vijñāna. This is translated as the "storehouse consciousness" (*ālaya-vijñāna*) because it is able to store the seeds of all phenomena that are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Due to these three meanings—namely: first, it is "that which stores," like a treasury of jewels, because it is able to contain and store all phenomena associated with outflows;

second, it is "that which is stored," because it is the locus for the seven preceding consciousnesses and their states of the three natures: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; third, it is "clinging" (*upādāna*).

The *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) takes the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the eighth consciousness as its object through the *darśana-bhāga* (perceptual aspect) of the seven consciousnesses, and it also grasps the *darśana-bhāga* of the eighth consciousness itself.

Because it is never separated from the four afflictions—namely, self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), self-pride (*ātma-māna*), self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), and self-love (*ātma-sneha*)—it now, within the state of Buddhahood, is transformed into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
It receives its name by way of analogy; that is to say, it is like a great perfect mirror.

Pervading the entire dharma-realm, its illuminating function is sovereign because it is free from all marks. As the Sixth Patriarch’s verse states: "The nature of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure;
the Equality Wisdom is a mind without affliction. The Wondrous Observing Wisdom reflects without effort; the Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks is identical to the Perfect Mirror.
By means of this discourse on the wondrous verse of the four wisdoms in their perfect fusion, they are subsumed and returned to one's own nature.
Suchness (tathatā). Because it is realized as conditioned and untainted (anāsrava), it does not fall within the categories of enumeration.

That which does not fall within enumeration refers to the severing of hindrances, the realization of truth, the entry into Great Perfect Enlightenment (mahābodhi), and the reaching of the other shore.

Regarding the person who cultivates the path through the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*), the commentary states: first, the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*); second, the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*);

third, the stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*); fourth, the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*); and fifth, the stage of culmination (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*). These constitute the five stages. As for "equipment" (*sambhāra*):

the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), and the ten transferences (*daśa-pratipatti*) constitute the state of worthiness (*satpuruṣa`), which is also called the stage of equipment. "Equipment" (*sam*) means assistance; "provisions" (*bhāra*) refers either to food or to the necessities for a journey.

It is a "provision" (sambhāra). Because one uses the provisions for the stages of faith, practice, abiding, progress, and penetration as sustenance to support the foundation of merit and wisdom of the ten bhūmis, it is called the stage of provisions (sambhāra-avasthā).

Regarding the "addition of practice" (prayoga): this refers to the cultivation of the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the Worldly Dharma after the three levels of the virtuous ones (tri-śukla).
This is called entering the stage of the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*); it is simply another name for diligence (*vīrya*).

"Thorough penetration" (*prativedha*) refers to first penetrating the three stages of the virtuous aids (*śuklavidarśana-bhūmi*) and subsequently penetrating the ten stages (*bhūmi*), as well as the two types of sublime awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); this is named the stage of thorough penetration. As for the "stage of cultivation" (*bhāvanā-avasthā*):

This refers to the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*), wherein one cultivates the *tathatā* (suchness) of the ten stages; one realizes that the six perfections are identical to the single mind and awakens to the fact that the myriad practices are identical to the single essence.

As for the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*): having transcended the ten stages and advanced to the two awakenings of Equality (*samatā*) and Wondrous Enlightenment (*pratyavekṣaṇā*), one severs the most subtle ignorance; this is called the ultimate stage.

Regarding the four heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the commentary states: First, the three heavens of the first dhyāna (*prathama-dhyāna*): 1) the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude (*brahmakāyika*);

2) the Heaven of the Brahma’s Ministers (*brahmapurohita*); 3) the Great Brahma Heaven (*mahābrahmā*). Second, the three heavens of the second dhyāna (*dvitīya-dhyāna*): 1) the Heaven of Limited Light (*parītta-ābhā*);

2) the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (*apramāṇa-ābhā*); 3) the Heaven of Radiant Sound (*ābhāsvara*). Third, the three heavens of the third dhyāna (*tṛtīya-dhyāna*): 1) the Heaven of Limited Purity (*parītta-śubha*); 2) the Heaven of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*); 3) the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (*apramāṇa-śubha*).
The four dhyānas comprise nine heavens: first, the Cloudless Heaven (*Anabhraka*); second, the Heaven of Merit-Born (*Puṇyaprasava*); third, the Heaven of Vast Results (*Bṛhatphala*);

and fourth, the Heaven of No-Thought (*Asaṃjñisattva*). This is the heaven of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Because the coarse perceptions of the six consciousnesses do not function there, they falsely reckon it to be *nirvāṇa*; thus it is named the Heaven of No-Thought.

The five heavens are: 1. the Heaven of No Affliction (Avṛha); 2. the Heaven of No Heat (Atapa); 3. the Heaven of Good Vision (Sudṛśa); 4. the Heaven of Good Appearance (Sudarśana); and 5. the Heaven of the Ultimate Form (Akaniṣṭha).
These five heavens above are called the Anāgāmin Heavens. In Sanskrit, *anāgāmin* means "one who does not return," referring to the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
These are the noble ones of the three fruits who have exhausted the nine grades of afflictions pertaining to thought (*saṃyojana*).

They do not return to take birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), but instead dwell in the heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) or the four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). [The commentary states: First, the Heaven of Infinite Space; second, the Heaven of Infinite Consciousness.
The third is the Heaven of Nothingness; the fourth is the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.

From the Untroubled Heaven (*Avṛha*) of the Form Realm up to the transcendence of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, if one does not conceive of a self, one realizes non-arising (*anutpāda*).

If one conceives of a self and grasps at realization, one falls into the views of external paths (*tīrthika*), being unable to sever delusions and realize the truth. Furthermore, regarding Bodhisattvas of the three stages...
Furthermore, by the power of the four dhyānas and eight samādhis, one is able to give rise to the light of boundless, wondrous wisdom;
thus, one advances to the fruit and virtue of the fourth bhūmi. As for the Buddha’s traversing [this path], he demonstrates the model for his later followers.
Regarding the power of the four dhyānas, the four emptinesses, and the eight attainments, the commentary states: First, the first dhyāna possesses three meanings.
First, the removal of hindrances, namely, sensual desires and unwholesome dharmas. Second, the cultivation of the antidote, namely, applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
Third, the benefit of cultivation, namely, the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion. The second dhyāna likewise has three [aspects]. First, the removal of hindrances, namely—
1. Cessation of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka* and *vicāra*). 2. Cultivation of the remedy: that is, internal tranquility of mind, being without applied or sustained thought.

3. Benefit of cultivation: this is called the stage of joy and bliss born of concentration (*samādhi*). The third dhyāna also possesses these three meanings: 1. Abandonment of hindrances: namely, the state of joy (*prīti*).
2. Cultivation of the remedy: possessing the three factors of mind. First, abiding in equanimity (*upekṣā*), because one has relinquished the state of joy. Second...

Right mindfulness, because there is no mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). Third, right knowledge (*samyak-jñāna*), because one attains pure and sublime bliss. These three meanings above constitute the antidote to the mind.
Fourth, the attainment of benefit is called the stage of sublime bliss free from joy (*niṣprītika-sukha-bhūmi*). The fourth dhyāna also possesses these three meanings:
first, the removal of obstacles, which means severing pleasure, previously eliminating pain, and the cessation of joy and sorrow; second, the cultivation of the antidote...

It is governed by neither-pain-nor-pleasure. These three attainments of benefit are called the Stage of Purity of Equanimity and Mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddhi-bhūmi*). Next, the four formless heavens (*ārūpya-deva*) are explained;

these are the heavens of the Formless Realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*). First, because those from the previous heavens of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) grow weary of desire and return to the Form Realm, this is the "form that is the fruit of meditative concentration" (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*).
Being free from the defiled characteristics of the Desire Realm, it is pure and subtle form, like the moon in water or flowers in the sky—without substantial reality.
Because of form (*rūpa*). Now, these devas further weary of form and return to emptiness; therefore, this heaven is named the Heaven of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).

Second, weary of space, they return to consciousness (*vijñāna*), thereby extinguishing the two objects of form and space. Since there is no coarse manifestation of the seventh consciousness (*manas*), this heaven possesses only half of it;
it is named the Heaven of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). Third, weary of consciousness, they return to the *ālaya*.
Yes. This refers to the stage where the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the seventh *manas*-consciousness no longer functions and the nature of the *ālaya-vijñāna* is gradually eliminated;

this is called the Heaven of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). At this fourth stage, one becomes weary of the nature of the *ālaya-vijñāna* because one perceives it as an obstruction, and thus turns away from it.

By investigating the nature of consciousness until nothing remains, one suddenly enters a state of profound stillness—how joyful this is! However, even in this heaven, there remains coarse conceptualization.

Although coarse perceptions have ceased, subtle perceptions have not yet been eliminated. As for those whose coarse perceptions have ceased, because these devas have exhausted the nature of consciousness, yet their subtle perceptions have not been eliminated, they still conceptually cling to the existence of a nature of nirvāṇa;
therefore, they are called the devas of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.

The *Commentary on the Emptiness of the Three Spheres* states: "Regarding the three spheres of body, speech, and mind, the Great Being realizes that his own self is its true mark (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Observing the body in this way, he observes the Buddha likewise; thus, the inner and outer three spheres are empty and quiescent.
Furthermore, because the giver, the recipient, and the intermediate gift are all entirely empty in their very essence, it is said that the three spheres are empty and quiescent."

The commentary on the two gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* states: first, the gate of *śamatha*; second, the gate of *vipaśyanā*. Now, regarding the first, the gate of *śamatha*, there are five [aspects]. First is the *śamatha* of ethical conduct (*śīla*).

This refers to the Bodhisattva’s threefold aggregate of precepts (*tri-vidha-saṃvara*), namely: the precept of restraining misconduct (*saṃvara-śīla*), the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*).
Because there is not even the slightest transgression against them, the Sanskrit term *vinaya* is translated here as [discipline].
First is the cessation of extinction: because it extinguishes all that is non-virtuous, this is called the cessation of ethical conduct (*śīla*). Second is the cessation of the place of reliance:
this refers to when a Great Being diligently cultivates the Supreme Vehicle and must distance themselves from clamor, fame, and gain;

dwelling in a forest hermitage (*araṇya*) is called the cessation of the place of reliance. Third is the cessation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*): this refers to the ancient masters who exclusively taught people to contemplate a single "critical phrase" (*huatou*).
Continuous and dense; intimate and earnest. Ultimately, what is this original face?
Thus looking and looking, doubting and doubting, investigating and investigating, one arrives at a state where there is nothing left to investigate.
Doubt reaches a point where there is nothing further to doubt. Walking is thus; sitting is thus; for a moment it is thus; sleeping is thus; dressing is thus;

eating is thus—even down to the smallest interval of time, a single hour, a single minute, or a single kṣaṇa—there is ultimately nothing in which one does not investigate and nothing in which one does not doubt. This is what is called "investigation" (chan).
When you reach a place where there is nothing to participate in, and when doubt reaches a place where there is nothing to doubt, suddenly the mass of doubt falls away.
You sit and cut off past and present with a single "keng" sound. It turns out to be a ready-made public case.

This is what is called "encountering the truth at every touch" and "standing alone as the illuminating essence," which is named the cessation of practice. This is the cessation that cuts off the four delusions. As the ancients said, "The Great Matter has not yet..."
"Clear as if mourning one's parents. Once the Great Matter has been clarified, one must once again act as if mourning one's parents.
After seeing the Way, one must necessarily be taught to contemplate and verify the mind-ground, or practice the true ultimate nature (*paramārtha-svabhāva*) of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).
As for what is called the "true ultimate nature," it is the vision of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that cuts off the limit of reality; it is what is meant by the Dharma not...

Having attained the realization of existence and non-existence, one first realizes the limit of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmatā*). One understands that not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended and enters the Bodhisattva stage of "Thorough Penetration" (*prativedha-avasthā*).
Therein, one beholds the pure Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and abandons the obstacles of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-āvaraṇa*), realizing the universally pervasive suchness (*sarvatraga-tathatā*).

One suddenly enters the great ocean of suchness where no other dharmas remain; thus, one realizes that the six perfections are but a single mind, severing [the notions of] arising, abiding, change, and cessation.

Having extinguished the ignorance of the four marks and severed them forever, one then realizes the stage of Great Perfect Enlightenment. This so-called realization is characterized by the absence of the mark of realization;

wisdom is characterized by the absence of the mark of wisdom. For the realized one alone, all is swept away without the slightest speck of dust; this is called "cessation through the eradication of delusions.

Regarding the five types of non-dual cessation, there are three: first, cessation through the realization of the true essence; second, cessation through skillful means following conditions; third, cessation through the stilling of the two extremes.

The analysis of cessation (*śamatha*). First, regarding the cessation of the true essence: because things arise where they are and are extinguished where they are, there is no place for movement or lingering attachment.
One realizes that all phenomena, from the very beginning, are free from the characteristics of verbal expression and free from the characteristics of mental objects;
they are indestructible and are nothing other than the single mind. This is called the cessation of the true essence. Second is the cessation of following conditions through skillful means.
One mobilizes a mind of immeasurable great compassion, benefiting sentient beings in every thought-moment, and cultivates the six perfections and myriad practices.
As thoughts arise, they are immediately stilled, like snow falling upon a red-hot furnace, melting away on the spot. This is called "stopping according with conditions through skillful means.
Third is "stopping the dualistic discrimination of thoughts": this refers to when a Bodhisattva enters the first stage (*bhūmi*) and advances through the second, third, and fourth stages.

One attains the *tathatā* (suchness) that is free from grasping. Moment by moment, one enters the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). When abandoning the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), this is the cessation of the conventional truth.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva enters the conventional truth, up until entering the seventh and eighth stages, they suddenly enter the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and realize the *tathatā* that neither increases nor decreases.
They abandon the obstacle to the manifestation of the wisdom of signless contemplation (*animitta-vipaśyanā-jñāna*) and sit [in meditative equipoise].
When even the mind that seeks nirvana is severed and purified, how much more so for those within the cycle of birth and death? This is called the cessation of the true reality (śamatha).
Next, proceeding from the eighth stage to the ninth and tenth stages, up to the stage of Equal and Wondrous Enlightenment, one realizes the mark of neither unity nor difference.

To be able to remain unchanging while following conditions, and to follow conditions while remaining unchanging—neither one nor many, neither arising nor ceasing—is called entering the wondrous, perfect ocean of *bodhi*.
This is the cessation that stops the discrimination of the two extremes.

Furthermore, the first part is the stage of seeing the Way (*darśanamārga*), the next is the stage of cultivating the Way (*bhāvanāmārga*), and the last is the stage of realizing the Way (*adhigamamārga*). What is called the stage of realizing the Way is precisely the conventional within the ultimate.

When expanded, it pervades the entire dharma-realm without exterior; thus, within the conventional, there is the ultimate. When contracted, it retracts and hides within the tip of a hair without interior;
the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma reaches this very point. This is what is called the cessation of non-duality.
Second, regarding the practitioner of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), there are three types. First is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). The *Awakening of Faith* states:

"To constantly contemplate the dharmas as suffering, empty, impermanent, non-self, and impure is called the contemplation of phenomenal practice (*vastu-caryā-vipaśyanā*). Furthermore, as for the contemplator of emptiness:

they realize that all dharmas are without self (*ātman*), without person (*pudgala*), without sentient beings (*sattva*), and without life-span (*jīva*), because the essence of dharmas is suchness (*tathatā*) and lacks intrinsic characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*).
This is because, as it is said: first, all is empty; thus, everything is empty. Second, the contemplation of the provisional:

one contemplates all phenomena as being like reflections of light in the past, like reflections of light in the future, and like reflections of light in the present. Furthermore, one contemplates all noble ones and ordinary beings in this same way.
The laws of cause and effect regarding worldly and world-transcending phenomena are like dreams, shadows, illusions, and reflections;
they resemble the moon in water or flowers in the sky because they lack substantial reality. Even *tathatā* (suchness) is but a provisional designation.
Why? Because the nature of *tathatā* takes "the absence of nature" as its nature; therefore, it too is like an illusion. As it is said:

Because the one is conventionally designated as all that is conventional. Regarding the "Middle Way" among these three: it means that the entire nature gives rise to cultivation, and the entirety of cultivation is itself the nature.
One realizes that the six perfections are identical to the single mind, and one awakens to the fact that wondrous conduct is identical to the single essence. It is neither one nor many.
It is like the pure full moon, solitary and without companion, such that it cannot be grasped by thought. This is because within one, all are contained.
Therefore, emptiness, the provisional, and the middle are the complete and perfect fusion of the whole;

this seamless fusion is the very ground of the vibrant activity of True Suchness (Tathatā). Thus, the three contemplations are identical to the three cessations, and the three cessations are identical to the three [contemplations].

Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Even up to that which is neither cessation (*śamatha*) nor contemplation—only one who is able to both cease and contemplate can enter the ocean of the *dharmadhātu*, the Great Radiant Treasury.

Regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and the three absence-of-nature (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*), the commentary states: First, the imputed nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) refers to the pervasive conceptualization of a single...

The characteristics of all phenomena and non-phenomena are like grasping at the objects of dreams and illusions as being truly existent; this is precisely the twofold clinging to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*).

Therefore, it is called the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Second, the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*) refers to the arising of function from essence, like water forming waves.
To grasp the characteristics of the waves as being truly existent is the nature of pervasive conceptualization; not grasping them [as such] is the nature of dependent origination.

"Characteristics" refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). If one subsumes its functions back into its essence, it is the dependent nature's lack of intrinsic existence, which is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Regarding the third, the perfected nature: it does not diminish in ordinary beings and does not increase in noble ones;

being neither deficient nor redundant, it is called "perfect" (*pari*). Furthermore, because it sustains the essential natures and characteristics of all phenomena, it is called [the perfected nature].

It is established as such because it is called "real" in contrast to the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*), which is false. The three natures each possess their own essence (*svabhāva*) that cannot be altered;

this is called "nature" (*dharmatā*). Therefore, it is named the "perfected real nature" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Furthermore, the nature of pervasive conceptualization exists in principle but does not exist in reality;
the characteristic of the dependent nature (*paratantra*) exists in reality but does not exist in principle; the perfected real nature exists both in principle and in reality.
There is none. Hence it is said: "the three natures, the three absences of nature," and so forth.
Regarding the "trichiliocosm" (three-thousandfold world system), the commentary states: when one set of four continents is fully completed, it is called a small thousand-world system.
When the number of these small thousands reaches one thousand, it is called a medium thousand-world system. Medium...

One thousand [units] constitute one thousand; when the count reaches one thousand, it is called a great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*). Because "thousand" is stated three times, it is named the "trichiliocosm.

There are twenty-four types of non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*): first, the homogeneous character of a group (*nikāyasabhāga*); second, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); third, acquisition (*prāpti*); fourth, the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
5. The attainment of non-conception; 6. The attainment of cessation; 7. Name-body; 8. Phrase; 9. Syllable;
10. Birth; 11. Aging; 12. Abiding; 13. Impermanence; 14. Transmigration; 15. Concentration and wisdom;
16. Succession; 17. Time; 18. Association; 19. Opposition of force; 20. Impurity; 21. [Continuation].
The "thin skin" consists of twenty-two factors. When combined with the twenty-three factors, there are twenty-four; when not combined, there are twenty-four as well.
That which is called "dissociated" (viprayukta) refers to the fact that apart from matter (rūpa) and mind (citta), there is no separate entity.
It is designated as "dissociated" because it is neither associated with the mind nor associated with matter.
It is said that these are not mutually exclusive.
Regarding the three minds, the commentary states: first, the direct mind, because it correctly contemplates the Dharma of True Suchness;
second, the profound mind, because it delights in practicing all wholesome dharmas; third, the mind of great compassion, because it universally rescues all sentient beings. Furthermore, the direct...
The first, the mind of aspiration (*cittotpāda*), subsumes the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Second, the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*) subsumes the ten practices (*caryā*).

Third, the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) subsumes the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*). If these three minds are cultivated simultaneously, they subsume the sublime practices of the ten stages.
If these three minds are fulfilled without remainder, they subsume the positions of both Equal and Sublime Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). In total, nothing transcends these three minds.

Thus, there are thirty-one kinds of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*): first, ten kinds of shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*), namely: long, short, square, round, coarse, fine, high, low, regular, and irregular;
second, eight kinds of indicative color (*vijñapti-rūpa*), namely: taking up, laying aside, contracting, extending, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down;
third, thirteen kinds of manifest color (*varṇa-rūpa*), namely: blue, yellow, red, white, light, shadow, brightness, darkness, clouds, smoke, dust, mist, and space.
The Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks are as follows: first, the soles of his feet are level like the bottom of a casket; second, the soles of his feet bear the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel;
third, his fingers and toes are long and surpass those of other men; fourth, his hands and feet are soft and supple; fifth, his fingers and toes are joined by a web-like membrane;
sixth, his heels are full and complete; seventh, his ankles are high and well-formed; eighth, his calves are like those of the eneya deer king. Ninth...
10. Standing upright, his hands reach his knees; 11. His male organ is concealed within a sheath like that of a horse-king; 12. The height and breadth of his body are equal; 13.
The hairs on his body grow upward, being blue-black in color and soft; 14. The hairs curl to the right; 15. He has a golden radiance.
15. The radiance of his body extends one *zhang* in every direction. 16. His skin is so fine and smooth that dust and water do not adhere to it. 17.
The two soles of his feet, the two palms of his hands, and the two shoulders—these seven places are full. 18. The area beneath both armpits is full.
19. His body is like that of a lion king. 20. His body is upright and straight. 21. His shoulders are rounded and well-formed. 22. The four...
20. He possesses a full set of forty teeth. 21. His teeth are white, pure, even, and closely set with deep roots.
22. His four canine teeth are white and large. 23. His jaw is like that of a lion. 24. He obtains the supreme flavor among all flavors.
27. His tongue is thin and broad, covering his face as far as the hairline. 28. His Brahma-voice is deep and resonant, like that of the kalaviṅka bird.
29. The color of his eyes is like refined gold. 30. His eyelashes are like those of a bull king. 31.
Between his eyebrows, he has a white tuft of hair (ūrṇā) like tūla-cotton. 32. On the crown of his head, he has a fleshy protuberance (uṣṇīṣa), whose marks are fully perfected.
